topics.title: Foundations: Formal Languages and Non-computability
topics.summary: Alphabets, strings, languages and their operations; grammars in outline; countability, Cantor's diagonal argument and Russell's paradox, and why almost every language is uncomputable.

blocks.text:
## What a formal language actually is

Theory of computation studies machines by studying the *sets of strings* they accept. Everything in the unit is built from three definitions, so it pays to get them exactly right.

An **alphabet** $\Sigma$ is a finite, non-empty set of symbols: $\{0,1\}$, $\{a,b\}$, the 128 ASCII characters. A **string** (or word) over $\Sigma$ is a finite sequence of symbols drawn from $\Sigma$. The **empty string** is written $\varepsilon$ and has length $0$; it is a perfectly good string, and $\varepsilon \ne \varnothing$ and $\{\varepsilon\} \ne \varnothing$. The **length** $|w|$ is the number of symbol occurrences, so $|abba| = 4$.

Notation you must be able to count with:

- $\Sigma^k$ is the set of strings of length exactly $k$, and $|\Sigma^k| = |\Sigma|^k$. In particular $\Sigma^0 = \{\varepsilon\}$, so $|\Sigma^0| = 1$, not $0$.
- $\Sigma^{*} = \Sigma^0 \cup \Sigma^1 \cup \Sigma^2 \cup \cdots$ — all finite strings, including $\varepsilon$.
- $\Sigma^{+} = \Sigma^{*} \setminus \{\varepsilon\}$ — all non-empty finite strings.

For $|\Sigma| = m$ the number of strings of length at most $n$ is the geometric sum

$$1 + m + m^2 + \cdots + m^n = \frac{m^{\,n+1}-1}{m-1} \quad (m > 1).$$

A **language** over $\Sigma$ is simply a subset $L \subseteq \Sigma^{*}$. It may be finite ($\{a, ab, bba\}$), infinite ($\{a^n b^n : n \ge 0\}$), empty ($\varnothing$), or everything ($\Sigma^{*}$). No meaning is attached to the strings; "the language of C programs that halt" is just a particular subset of ASCII strings.

Two points that the examiner leans on. First, $\Sigma^{*}$ is an infinite set, but every element of it is a *finite* string — there is no infinite string in $\Sigma^{*}$. Second, a language is a set of strings, while a *class* of languages (regular, context-free, recursive) is a set of sets of strings; "regular" is a property of a language, never of a string.

## Operations on languages

Because languages are sets, all set operations apply: union $L_1 \cup L_2$, intersection $L_1 \cap L_2$, difference $L_1 - L_2$, and **complement** $\bar{L} = \Sigma^{*} - L$, which is only meaningful once $\Sigma$ is fixed.

String-specific operations:

| Operation | Definition |
|---|---|
| Concatenation | $L_1 L_2 = \{xy : x \in L_1,\ y \in L_2\}$ |
| Power | $L^0 = \{\varepsilon\}$, $L^{k+1} = L^k L$ |
| Kleene star | $L^{*} = \bigcup_{k \ge 0} L^k$ |
| Positive closure | $L^{+} = \bigcup_{k \ge 1} L^k$ |
| Reversal | $L^R = \{w^R : w \in L\}$ |
| Homomorphism | $h(L) = \{h(w) : w \in L\}$ where $h$ maps each symbol to a string |

Because $L^0 = \{\varepsilon\}$ by definition, $L^{*}$ **always contains $\varepsilon$**, whatever $L$ is. And $L^{+} = L L^{*} = L^{*} L$, with $\varepsilon \in L^{+}$ if and only if $\varepsilon \in L$. Hence $L^{*} = L^{+} \cup \{\varepsilon\}$ always, but $L^{+} = L^{*} - \{\varepsilon\}$ only when $\varepsilon \notin L$.

The two identities most often tested:

$$\varnothing^{*} = \{\varepsilon\}, \qquad \{\varepsilon\}^{*} = \{\varepsilon\}, \qquad \varnothing^{+} = \varnothing.$$

$$L \varnothing = \varnothing \varnothing = \varnothing, \qquad L\{\varepsilon\} = L, \qquad L \cup \varnothing = L.$$

So $\varnothing$ is the identity for union and the annihilator for concatenation, while $\{\varepsilon\}$ is the identity for concatenation. Writing $L\varnothing = L$ is the single commonest slip in this area: concatenating with the empty *set* gives no strings at all, because there is no second half to choose.

## Grammars in outline

A **grammar** generates a language instead of accepting one. Formally $G = (V, T, P, S)$ where $V$ is the finite set of variables (non-terminals), $T$ the finite set of terminals with $V \cap T = \varnothing$, $S \in V$ the start symbol, and $P$ a finite set of productions $\alpha \to \beta$ with $\alpha, \beta \in (V \cup T)^{*}$ and $\alpha$ containing at least one variable.

One **derivation step** $\gamma \alpha \delta \Rightarrow \gamma \beta \delta$ replaces an occurrence of $\alpha$ by $\beta$. Write $\Rightarrow^{*}$ for zero or more steps. The generated language is

$$L(G) = \{ w \in T^{*} : S \Rightarrow^{*} w \}.$$

Note $w$ must consist of **terminals only**; a string still containing variables is a *sentential form*, not a sentence. Restricting the shape of the productions gives the four Chomsky types — type 0 unrestricted, type 1 context-sensitive, type 2 context-free, type 3 regular — which are developed properly in topic 8.4. For now, the important idea is the pairing: every class of grammars has a matching class of machines, and the whole unit is the table of those pairings.

## There are more languages than programs

Here is the result that makes the rest of computability inevitable, and it is pure counting.

A set is **countable** if it is finite or can be put in bijection with $\mathbb{N}$ — equivalently, if its elements can be listed as $x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots$ so that every element appears at some finite position.

**$\Sigma^{*}$ is countable.** List the strings in **shortlex** (canonical) order: all strings of length 0, then all of length 1 in alphabetical order, then all of length 2, and so on. For $\Sigma = \{0,1\}$ this gives

$$\varepsilon,\ 0,\ 1,\ 00,\ 01,\ 10,\ 11,\ 000,\ 001, \ldots$$

Each length class is finite (size $m^k$), so every string is reached after finitely many steps. This matters: plain dictionary order does **not** work, because $0, 00, 000, 0000, \ldots$ would come before $1$ and the listing would never reach $1$.

**The set of all programs is countable.** A program in any fixed language is a finite string over a finite character set, so the programs form a subset of $\Sigma^{*}$, and a subset of a countable set is countable. The same argument covers Turing machines: a TM has a finite description, so TMs can be encoded as strings and enumerated $M_1, M_2, M_3, \ldots$.

**The set of all languages over $\Sigma$ is uncountable.** Languages over $\Sigma$ are exactly the subsets of $\Sigma^{*}$, i.e. the power set $2^{\Sigma^{*}}$, and Cantor's theorem says $|2^{A}| > |A|$ for every set $A$. So there are strictly more languages than there are strings, hence strictly more languages than programs.

The conclusion is immediate and devastating. Programs are countably infinite; languages are uncountably infinite; so **almost every language has no program that decides it**, and indeed no Turing machine that even recognises it. The argument is non-constructive — it names no particular undecidable language — but it guarantees that undecidability is the norm rather than a curiosity. Topic 8.5 then exhibits concrete examples such as the halting problem.

blocks.title: Worked example — Cantor diagonalisation on a table of languages
blocks.text:
Suppose, for contradiction, that every language over $\Sigma = \{0,1\}$ could be listed as $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$. List the strings in shortlex order as $w_1 = \varepsilon$, $w_2 = 0$, $w_3 = 1$, $w_4 = 00$, and so on, and build the infinite $0/1$ table

$$M[i][j] = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } w_j \in L_i \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Take a concrete opening fragment:

| | $w_1=\varepsilon$ | $w_2=0$ | $w_3=1$ | $w_4=00$ | $w_5=01$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $L_1$ | **1** | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| $L_2$ | 0 | **0** | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| $L_3$ | 1 | 1 | **1** | 0 | 0 |
| $L_4$ | 0 | 1 | 0 | **0** | 1 |
| $L_5$ | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 | **1** |

Now define the **diagonal language**

$$D = \{\, w_i : w_i \notin L_i \,\},$$

i.e. take the bold diagonal $1,0,1,0,1$ and flip every bit to get $0,1,0,1,0$. So $\varepsilon \notin D$, $0 \in D$, $1 \notin D$, $00 \in D$, $01 \notin D$, and so on.

$D$ is a perfectly legitimate language — it is some subset of $\Sigma^{*}$. But $D \ne L_1$, because they disagree on $w_1$; $D \ne L_2$, because they disagree on $w_2$; in general $D \ne L_i$ because $w_i \in D \iff w_i \notin L_i$. So $D$ appears nowhere in the supposedly complete list, contradicting the assumption. Therefore no enumeration of all languages exists: $2^{\Sigma^{*}}$ is uncountable.

**The same machine, aimed at Turing machines.** Enumerate all TMs as $M_1, M_2, \ldots$ and all strings as $w_1, w_2, \ldots$, and set $M[i][j] = 1$ iff $M_i$ accepts $w_j$. The diagonal language $L_d = \{ w_i : M_i \text{ does not accept } w_i \}$ differs from the language of every $M_i$ at the string $w_i$, so **no Turing machine accepts $L_d$** — $L_d$ is not even recursively enumerable. That single construction, and not any deep property of computation, is where the halting problem comes from.

blocks.title: Russell's paradox — the same trick in set theory
blocks.text:
Naive set theory allows a set to be defined by any property. Consider

$$R = \{\, S : S \notin S \,\},$$

the set of all sets that are not members of themselves. Ask whether $R \in R$. If $R \in R$, then $R$ satisfies the defining property, so $R \notin R$. If $R \notin R$, then it satisfies the property, so $R \in R$. Both branches contradict, so $R$ cannot exist, and unrestricted set comprehension is inconsistent.

The popular version is the **barber paradox**: the village barber shaves exactly those men who do not shave themselves; who shaves the barber?

Structurally this is identical to diagonalisation and to the halting-problem proof. In each case you build an object whose behaviour on *itself* is defined to be the opposite of what it is, and the contradiction kills the assumption that produced it — respectively "all sets exist", "all languages can be listed", and "a halting-decider exists".

## Decision problems are languages

A **decision problem** is a yes/no question about an input: "is this graph 3-colourable?", "does this program halt on this input?" Fix an encoding of instances as strings (written $\langle G \rangle$, $\langle M, w \rangle$, and so on). The problem then *is* the language of its yes-instances:

$$L_{\text{3COL}} = \{ \langle G \rangle : G \text{ is 3-colourable} \}.$$

Solving the problem means deciding membership in that language, which is why "algorithm" and "automaton" can be used interchangeably throughout the unit. Three degrees of solvability will be distinguished in topic 8.4:

- **Recursive (decidable)** — some TM halts on every input, answering yes or no.
- **Recursively enumerable (semi-decidable)** — some TM halts and accepts on every yes-instance, but may loop forever on a no-instance.
- **Not even RE** — no TM recognises it at all; the diagonal language $L_d$ above is the standard example.

The counting argument tells us most languages fall in the last bucket. It also justifies a convenient habit: whenever a question says "is problem $X$ decidable?", rewrite $X$ as a language first, because every technique in topic 8.5 — reduction, Rice's theorem, closure under complement — is stated about languages.

blocks.q: Which of the following is **false**?
blocks.exp: Concatenation pairs a string from the left language with one from the right. If the right language is empty there is no second half to choose, so $L\varnothing = \varnothing$, not $L$. The empty *set* annihilates under concatenation; the set $\{\varepsilon\}$ containing the empty *string* is the identity. The other three are standard: $\varnothing^{*} = \varnothing^{0} = \{\varepsilon\}$, and $L^{0}=\{\varepsilon\} \subseteq L^{*}$.

blocks.q: Which statement correctly summarises the counting argument for the existence of non-recursively-enumerable languages?
opts: Both the set of Turing machines and the set of languages over $\{0,1\}$ are uncountable, but the languages are 'more' uncountable
The set of Turing machines is countable while the set of languages over $\{0,1\}$ is uncountable, so some language has no accepting machine
The set of Turing machines is uncountable while the set of languages is countable
Both sets are countably infinite, so a bijection exists and every language is recognisable
blocks.exp: A Turing machine has a finite description, so machines can be encoded as finite strings and listed — countably many. Languages over $\{0,1\}$ are the subsets of $\{0,1\}^{*}$, and by Cantor's theorem the power set of a countably infinite set is uncountable. An uncountable collection cannot be covered by a countable one, so languages with no machine at all must exist.

blocks.q: Over $\Sigma = \{a,b,c\}$, how many strings have length at most 3?
blocks.exp: Count by length: $3^0 + 3^1 + 3^2 + 3^3 = 1 + 3 + 9 + 27 = 40$. The geometric formula gives the same thing: $(3^{4}-1)/(3-1) = 80/2 = 40$. The commonest error is forgetting the single string of length $0$, namely $\varepsilon$, which gives 39.

tricks.title: Count strings with the geometric sum, never by listing
tricks.body: For $|\Sigma| = m$: exactly $n$ long gives $m^n$; at most $n$ long gives $\dfrac{m^{n+1}-1}{m-1}$. Always add the one string of length $0$. For binary, "at most $n$" is just $2^{n+1} - 1$.

tricks.title: $\varnothing$ and $\{\varepsilon\}$ behave like 0 and 1
tricks.body: Concatenation acts like multiplication and union like addition: $L \cdot \varnothing = \varnothing$ (times zero), $L \cdot \{\varepsilon\} = L$ (times one), $L \cup \varnothing = L$ (plus zero). Every identity in this area falls out of that analogy.

tricks.title: Shortlex order is the only enumeration that works
tricks.body: Whenever a question asks you to enumerate $\Sigma^{*}$ or to index strings $w_1, w_2, \ldots$, order by length first and alphabetically within a length. Dictionary order stalls on $0, 00, 000, \ldots$ and never reaches $1$, so it is not an enumeration at all.

tricks.title: Spot diagonalisation by the phrase 'differs from the $i$-th at position $i$'
tricks.body: Cantor's proof, Russell's paradox, the diagonal language $L_d$ and the halting-problem proof are one argument in four costumes. If a question describes an object built to disagree with the $i$-th item at the $i$-th place, the answer is always "no such enumeration / no such machine exists".

tricks.title: Turn every decidability question into a language question first
tricks.body: Write the problem as $\{\langle \cdot \rangle : \text{property holds}\}$ before reasoning. Closure properties, reductions and Rice's theorem are all stated about languages, and half of the difficulty of complexity questions is failing to make that translation.

traps.title: $\varepsilon$, $\{\varepsilon\}$ and $\varnothing$ are three different things
traps.body: $\varepsilon$ is a string of length 0; $\{\varepsilon\}$ is a language containing exactly that one string, so its size is 1; $\varnothing$ is a language containing no strings, so its size is 0. A regular expression matching $\varnothing$ accepts nothing; one matching $\varepsilon$ accepts one string. Examiners test this with $\varnothing^{*} = \{\varepsilon\}$ and with $L\varnothing = \varnothing$.

traps.title: 'Infinite language' does not mean 'infinite strings'
traps.body: Every string in $\Sigma^{*}$ is finite. A language can contain infinitely many strings, each of finite length; no string of infinite length is ever a member. Consequently every string in an infinite language can be pumped or parsed in finitely many steps, which is what makes the pumping lemma possible at all.

traps.title: The counting argument proves existence, not an example
traps.body: 'There are uncountably many languages and countably many machines' shows undecidable languages exist but identifies none. To show a *specific* language undecidable you need diagonalisation or a reduction. A question asking 'which argument proves the halting problem undecidable?' wants diagonalisation, not cardinality.

traps.title: A subset of a countable set is countable, not necessarily finite
traps.body: Students sometimes conclude that because the set of programs is countable, it is small or finite. It is countably *infinite*. The point is not scarcity of programs but the far greater abundance of languages.

blocks.text:
## Finite automata: the machine with no memory but its state

A finite automaton is a program with a fixed, finite amount of memory. It reads the input once, left to right, never writes anything, and its entire knowledge of the past is the single state it is currently in. Everything a regular language can do, and every limitation it has, follows from that one sentence.

A **deterministic finite automaton** is $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ with $Q$ a finite set of states, $\Sigma$ the input alphabet, $\delta : Q \times \Sigma \to Q$ a *total* function, $q_0 \in Q$ the start state and $F \subseteq Q$ the accepting states. Extend $\delta$ to strings by $\hat\delta(q, \varepsilon) = q$ and $\hat\delta(q, xa) = \delta(\hat\delta(q,x), a)$; then $L(M) = \{ w : \hat\delta(q_0, w) \in F \}$.

"Total" is the word that matters. A DFA has **exactly one** transition out of every state on every symbol. A diagram with a missing arrow is not yet a DFA; it becomes one by adding a non-accepting **dead (trap) state** that loops to itself on everything. A DFA with $n$ states drawn without its dead state really has $n+1$.

A **non-deterministic finite automaton** relaxes this to $\delta : Q \times \Sigma \to 2^{Q}$: zero, one or many successors. The NFA accepts $w$ if **some** computation path ends in an accepting state. An **$\varepsilon$-NFA** further allows $\delta : Q \times (\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\}) \to 2^{Q}$, taking transitions without consuming input.

The three models accept exactly the same class of languages — the **regular** languages. Non-determinism buys conciseness, never power. The cost is state count: an $n$-state NFA may need up to $2^{n}$ DFA states, and for the language "the $n$-th symbol from the end is $1$" that bound is actually attained, with an $(n+1)$-state NFA against a $2^{n}$-state minimal DFA.

## $\varepsilon$-closure and subset construction

To convert an $\varepsilon$-NFA to a DFA you need $\varepsilon$-closure. For a state $q$, $\text{ECLOSE}(q)$ is $q$ together with everything reachable from $q$ using $\varepsilon$-transitions only; for a set, take the union. Always include the state itself, and keep following $\varepsilon$-arrows until nothing new appears.

**Subset construction** (also called the powerset construction) builds a DFA whose states are *sets* of NFA states:

- Start state: $\text{ECLOSE}(\{q_0\})$ (just $\{q_0\}$ if there are no $\varepsilon$-moves).
- Transition: $\delta_D(S, a) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\bigcup_{q \in S} \delta_N(q, a)\right)$.
- Accepting: $S$ is accepting iff $S \cap F_N \ne \varnothing$.
- The empty set $\varnothing$ is a legitimate DFA state — it is the dead state, and it loops to itself on every symbol.

The right way to run it in an exam is **lazily**: start from the start set and generate only the subsets that actually appear. The theoretical bound is $2^{n}$ states, but the number *reachable* is usually far smaller, and a question asking "how many states does the resulting DFA have?" nearly always means reachable states.

blocks.title: Worked example — subset construction, with and without $\varepsilon$
blocks.text:
**(a) NFA with no $\varepsilon$-moves.** $Q = \{q_0,q_1,q_2\}$, $\Sigma = \{a,b\}$, start $q_0$, $F = \{q_2\}$:

| | $a$ | $b$ |
|---|---|---|
| $q_0$ | $\{q_0,q_1\}$ | $\{q_0\}$ |
| $q_1$ | $\varnothing$ | $\{q_2\}$ |
| $q_2$ | $\varnothing$ | $\varnothing$ |

Start subset $A = \{q_0\}$.

- $\delta(A,a) = \{q_0,q_1\} = B$; $\delta(A,b) = \{q_0\} = A$.
- $B = \{q_0,q_1\}$: on $a$, $\delta(q_0,a) \cup \delta(q_1,a) = \{q_0,q_1\} \cup \varnothing = B$; on $b$, $\{q_0\} \cup \{q_2\} = \{q_0,q_2\} = C$.
- $C = \{q_0,q_2\}$: on $a$, $\{q_0,q_1\} \cup \varnothing = B$; on $b$, $\{q_0\} \cup \varnothing = A$.

Nothing new appears, so the DFA has 3 reachable states out of a possible $2^3 = 8$:

| | $a$ | $b$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\to A$ | $B$ | $A$ |
| $B$ | $B$ | $C$ |
| $*C$ | $B$ | $A$ |

Only $C$ contains $q_2$, so $C$ is the single accepting state. Reading it off: the DFA is in $B$ exactly after an $a$, and in $C$ exactly after $\ldots ab$. The language is **strings ending in $ab$**, which is what the NFA was guessing at.

**(b) $\varepsilon$-NFA.** $Q = \{0,1,2\}$, $\Sigma = \{a,b,c\}$, start $0$, $F = \{2\}$, with $\varepsilon$-arrows $0 \to 1$ and $1 \to 2$, and self-loops $0 \xrightarrow{a} 0$, $1 \xrightarrow{b} 1$, $2 \xrightarrow{c} 2$.

$\text{ECLOSE}(0) = \{0,1,2\}$, $\text{ECLOSE}(1) = \{1,2\}$, $\text{ECLOSE}(2) = \{2\}$.

Start $A = \text{ECLOSE}(0) = \{0,1,2\}$.

- $\delta(A,a)$: moves on $a$ from $\{0,1,2\}$ give $\{0\}$; $\text{ECLOSE}(\{0\}) = \{0,1,2\} = A$.
- $\delta(A,b)$: moves give $\{1\}$; $\text{ECLOSE}(\{1\}) = \{1,2\} = B$.
- $\delta(A,c)$: moves give $\{2\}$; $\text{ECLOSE}(\{2\}) = \{2\} = C$.
- $B = \{1,2\}$: on $a$, no moves $\Rightarrow \varnothing = D$ (dead); on $b$, $\{1\} \Rightarrow B$; on $c$, $\{2\} \Rightarrow C$.
- $C = \{2\}$: on $a$ and $b$, $\varnothing = D$; on $c$, $C$.
- $D = \varnothing$ goes to $D$ on everything.

$A$, $B$ and $C$ all contain state $2$, so all three accept; $D$ does not. The DFA accepts $a^{*}b^{*}c^{*}$ — exactly what the chain of $\varepsilon$-arrows was expressing.

blocks.text:
## Minimisation by table filling

Every regular language has a **unique** minimal DFA, up to renaming of states — a consequence of the Myhill-Nerode theorem, which says the minimal number of states equals the number of equivalence classes of the relation "$x \equiv_L y$ iff for every $z$, $xz \in L \iff yz \in L$". Uniqueness is why "the minimal DFA" is a well-posed exam question with one numeric answer.

The **table-filling (Moore) algorithm** finds it:

Two states $p, q$ are **distinguishable** if some string $z$ sends exactly one of them into $F$; otherwise they are **equivalent** and may be merged.

items: Remove all states unreachable from the start state. They can never affect the language, and table filling will not remove them for you.
Make the automaton complete: if any transition is missing, add a dead state.
Draw a lower-triangular table with one cell per unordered pair of states.
Basis: mark every pair (final, non-final). These are distinguished by $z = \varepsilon$.
Induction: for each unmarked pair $(p,q)$ and each symbol $a$, if the pair $(\delta(p,a), \delta(q,a))$ is already marked, mark $(p,q)$.
Repeat step 5 until a whole pass marks nothing new.
Unmarked pairs are equivalent. Merge each equivalence class into one state; transitions are well defined because equivalent states go to equivalent states.

blocks.title: Worked example — minimising an 8-state DFA
blocks.text:
$\Sigma = \{0,1\}$, start $A$, $F = \{C\}$.

| state | 0 | 1 |
|---|---|---|
| $\to A$ | $B$ | $F$ |
| $B$ | $G$ | $C$ |
| $*C$ | $A$ | $C$ |
| $D$ | $C$ | $G$ |
| $E$ | $H$ | $F$ |
| $F$ | $C$ | $G$ |
| $G$ | $G$ | $E$ |
| $H$ | $G$ | $C$ |

**Step 1 — reachability.** From $A$: $A \to B, F$; $B \to G, C$; $F \to C, G$; $G \to G, E$; $C \to A, C$; $E \to H, F$; $H \to G, C$. Reached: $A,B,C,E,F,G,H$. **$D$ is unreachable** and is deleted at once. (Leaving it in is the classic way to get the wrong state count: $D$ would merge with $F$, which changes nothing about the language but does change your answer if you also forget to delete it.)

**Step 2 — basis.** $C$ is the only final state, so mark $(C,X)$ for all $X \ne C$.

**Step 3 — first induction pass.** On input $1$, the states going to $C$ are $B$ and $H$; on input $0$, the state going to $C$ is $F$. Any pair that splits one of those groups gets marked:

- via input $1$: $(A,B), (A,H), (B,E), (B,F), (B,G), (E,H), (F,H), (G,H)$
- via input $0$: $(A,F), (E,F), (F,G)$

Surviving unmarked pairs: $(A,E), (A,G), (E,G), (B,H)$.

**Step 4 — second pass.**

- $(A,G)$: on $0$, $A \to B$ and $G \to G$; $(B,G)$ is marked $\Rightarrow$ **mark $(A,G)$**.
- $(E,G)$: on $0$, $E \to H$ and $G \to G$; $(G,H)$ is marked $\Rightarrow$ **mark $(E,G)$**.
- $(A,E)$: on $0$, $(B,H)$ — unmarked; on $1$, $(F,F)$ — same state. Nothing to mark.
- $(B,H)$: on $0$, $(G,G)$; on $1$, $(C,C)$. Identical successors, never markable.

**Step 5 — third pass** marks nothing, so stop.

**Equivalence classes:** $\{A,E\}$, $\{B,H\}$, $\{C\}$, $\{F\}$, $\{G\}$ — **5 states**, down from 8.

Minimal DFA, writing $P=\{A,E\}$, $Q=\{B,H\}$, $R=\{C\}$, $S=\{F\}$, $T=\{G\}$:

| state | 0 | 1 |
|---|---|---|
| $\to P$ | $Q$ | $S$ |
| $Q$ | $T$ | $R$ |
| $*R$ | $P$ | $R$ |
| $S$ | $R$ | $T$ |
| $T$ | $T$ | $P$ |

Check the merge is consistent: $A \xrightarrow{0} B$ and $E \xrightarrow{0} H$, and $B, H$ are in the same class $Q$ — good; $A \xrightarrow{1} F$ and $E \xrightarrow{1} F$ — good. Equivalent states always map to equivalent states, which is exactly why the quotient automaton is well defined.

## Regular expressions and their identities

Regular expressions are the algebra that matches the machines. The base cases are $\varnothing$, $\varepsilon$ and each $a \in \Sigma$; the operators are union $+$ (some books write $\mid$), concatenation, and Kleene star, with precedence **star > concatenation > union**. So $ab^{*}+c$ means $(a(b^{*})) + c$.

Kleene's theorem: a language is regular iff it is denoted by some regular expression. Thompson's construction turns an expression into an $\varepsilon$-NFA with at most $2m$ states for $m$ operator/operand occurrences; state elimination or Arden's theorem goes the other way.

Identities worth knowing cold:

| Identity | Comment |
|---|---|
| $r + r = r$ | union is idempotent |
| $r + s = s + r$, $(r+s)+t = r+(s+t)$ | union is commutative and associative |
| $(rs)t = r(st)$ | concatenation is associative but **not commutative** |
| $r(s+t) = rs + rt$, $(s+t)r = sr + tr$ | distributes both ways |
| $\varepsilon r = r\varepsilon = r$, $\varnothing r = r \varnothing = \varnothing$, $r + \varnothing = r$ | identities and annihilator |
| $(r^{*})^{*} = r^{*}$ | star is idempotent |
| $\varepsilon + r r^{*} = \varepsilon + r^{*} r = r^{*}$ | the unrolling law |
| $r^{+} = r r^{*} = r^{*} r$, $r^{*} = r^{+} + \varepsilon$ | |
| $(r+s)^{*} = (r^{*}s^{*})^{*} = (r^{*}+s^{*})^{*} = (r^{*}s)^{*}r^{*}$ | all four denote the same language |
| $r(sr)^{*} = (rs)^{*}r$ | the shifting law |
| $(\varnothing)^{*} = \varepsilon$, $(\varepsilon)^{*} = \varepsilon$ | |

Two non-identities to keep separate: $(rs)^{*} \ne r^{*}s^{*}$ (the left side forces alternation, the right does not: $aabb \in a^{*}b^{*}$ but $aabb \notin (ab)^{*}$), and $(r+s)^{*} \ne r^{*} + s^{*}$ (the left contains $ab$, the right does not).

**Arden's theorem.** If $P$ and $Q$ are regular expressions and $\varepsilon \notin L(P)$, then the equation $R = Q + RP$ has the unique solution $R = QP^{*}$. This is how you convert a finite automaton into an expression by writing one equation per state ("$R_i$ = everything that reaches state $i$") and back-substituting. The condition $\varepsilon \notin L(P)$ is essential: if $P$ could be $\varepsilon$ the equation has many solutions.

## Regular grammars

A grammar is **right-linear** if every production has the form $A \to wB$ or $A \to w$ with $w \in T^{*}$ and $A,B$ variables — at most one variable, always at the right end. It is **left-linear** if every production is $A \to Bw$ or $A \to w$ — at most one variable, always at the left end. Either kind alone generates exactly the regular languages, and these are the type-3 grammars.

Converting a right-linear grammar to an NFA is mechanical: one state per variable, plus a final state $Z$; a production $A \to aB$ becomes $A \xrightarrow{a} B$; $A \to a$ becomes $A \xrightarrow{a} Z$; $A \to \varepsilon$ makes $A$ final. Going the other way, each transition $p \xrightarrow{a} q$ becomes $P \to aQ$, and each final state $q$ contributes $Q \to \varepsilon$.

The trap: a grammar that mixes left-linear and right-linear productions is **not** regular in general. $S \to aS \mid Sb \mid \varepsilon$ looks harmless but is a linear, not a regular, grammar; here it happens to generate $a^{*}b^{*}$, which is regular, but $S \to aSb \mid \varepsilon$ — one variable, still "linear" — generates $a^{n}b^{n}$, which is not. Linear $\ne$ regular.

## Closure properties of regular languages

The regular languages are closed under **everything** normally asked about:

union, intersection, complement, set difference, symmetric difference, concatenation, Kleene star, positive closure, reversal, homomorphism, inverse homomorphism, substitution, quotient with an arbitrary language, and prefix/suffix/subsequence operations.

The useful constructions behind the list: complement by swapping $F$ and $Q - F$ **in a complete DFA**; intersection by the product automaton on $Q_1 \times Q_2$ with $F = F_1 \times F_2$ (use $F = (F_1 \times Q_2) \cup (Q_1 \times F_2)$ for union); difference as $L_1 \cap \overline{L_2}$.

Closure is the sharpest tool for *disproving* regularity. If $L$ were regular then any regular-preserving combination of $L$ with known regular languages would also be regular; find one that produces a known non-regular language and you are done. For instance, if $L = \{w \in \{a,b\}^{*} : \#_a(w) = \#_b(w)\}$ were regular then $L \cap a^{*}b^{*} = \{a^{n}b^{n}\}$ would be regular, which it is not.

Two facts that quietly follow: every **finite** language is regular (write it as a finite union of single strings), and therefore a language cannot be non-regular for having "too few" strings — only an infinite language can be non-regular. Also, adding or deleting finitely many strings never changes regularity.

## The pumping lemma, stated exactly

**Statement.** If $L$ is regular, then there exists a constant $p \ge 1$ (the pumping length) such that every string $w \in L$ with $|w| \ge p$ can be written $w = xyz$ with

1. $|xy| \le p$,
2. $|y| \ge 1$,
3. $xy^{i}z \in L$ for **every** $i \ge 0$.

The proof is the pigeonhole principle: run the minimal DFA on $w$; reading $p = $ (number of states) symbols visits $p+1$ states, so some state repeats within the first $p$ symbols; the loop between the two visits is $y$, and you may go round it any number of times.

**What it is and is not.** The lemma gives a *necessary* condition for regularity, not a sufficient one. So:

- $L$ regular $\Rightarrow$ $L$ is pumpable. Contrapositive: $L$ not pumpable $\Rightarrow$ $L$ not regular. **This is the only direction you may use.**
- $L$ pumpable $\not\Rightarrow$ $L$ regular. There are non-regular languages that satisfy the lemma perfectly.

## Playing it as an adversary game

Students misuse this lemma more than any other result in the syllabus, and the cure is to treat the proof as a two-player game where **you choose second at every step that matters**. To prove $L$ is *not* regular:

| Move | Who chooses | You must handle |
|---|---|---|
| 1. the pumping length $p$ | **adversary** | every possible $p$ — keep it symbolic, never set $p = 5$ |
| 2. the string $w \in L$, $|w| \ge p$ | **you** | pick one string, in terms of $p$, that traps the adversary |
| 3. the split $w = xyz$ with $\|xy\| \le p$, $\|y\| \ge 1$ | **adversary** | every legal split — enumerate the cases or use $\|xy\| \le p$ to force one |
| 4. the exponent $i$ | **you** | one value of $i$ suffices; $i = 0$ or $i = 2$ almost always works |

You win — and $L$ is non-regular — if for every $p$ you can name a $w$ such that for every legal split there is an $i$ with $xy^{i}z \notin L$.

The two fatal errors follow directly from the table. Choosing $y$ yourself is illegal, because the adversary chooses the split; all you may do is *constrain* the adversary using $|xy| \le p$. And finding one $i$ that keeps the string in $L$ proves nothing, because you need one $i$ that throws it out.

blocks.title: Worked example — three pumping-lemma proofs
blocks.text:
**(a) $L = \{a^{n}b^{n} : n \ge 0\}$ is not regular.**

Let the adversary give any $p \ge 1$. Choose $w = a^{p}b^{p}$; clearly $w \in L$ and $|w| = 2p \ge p$.

The adversary splits $w = xyz$ with $|xy| \le p$ and $|y| \ge 1$. Because the first $p$ symbols of $w$ are all $a$'s, the constraint $|xy| \le p$ **forces** $x$ and $y$ to lie entirely inside the $a$-block. So $x = a^{s}$, $y = a^{t}$ with $t \ge 1$, $s + t \le p$, and $z = a^{p-s-t}b^{p}$.

Choose $i = 2$: $xy^{2}z = a^{s}a^{2t}a^{p-s-t}b^{p} = a^{p+t}b^{p}$. Since $t \ge 1$, the counts differ, so $xy^{2}z \notin L$. ($i = 0$ works just as well, giving $a^{p-t}b^{p}$.) Every legal split fails, so $L$ is not regular.

Notice what the good choice of $w$ bought: because the whole first block is $a$'s, there is only **one case**, and the adversary's freedom evaporated. Had we chosen $w = (ab)^{p/2}\ldots$ we would have had messy cases for nothing.

**(b) $L = \{a^{i}b^{j} : i > j \ge 0\}$ is not regular.**

Given $p$, choose $w = a^{p+1}b^{p}$. Again $|xy| \le p$ forces $y = a^{t}$, $t \ge 1$, inside the $a$-block. Choose $i = 0$: $xy^{0}z = a^{p+1-t}b^{p}$. Since $t \ge 1$, $p+1-t \le p$, so the number of $a$'s is no longer greater than the number of $b$'s, and the string leaves $L$. Here $i=2$ would **not** work — more $a$'s keeps the string in $L$ — which is exactly why the exponent is yours to choose and why one good $i$ is all you need.

**(c) $L = \{ww^{R} : w \in \{a,b\}^{*}\}$, the even-length palindromes, is not regular.**

Given $p$, choose $w = a^{p}b\,b\,a^{p}$, which is $uu^{R}$ for $u = a^{p}b$ and has length $2p+2 \ge p$. The prefix constraint $|xy| \le p$ again puts $y = a^{t}$, $t \ge 1$, inside the leading $a$-block. Pumping to $i = 2$ gives $a^{p+t}bba^{p}$, which is not a palindrome because it starts with $p+t$ $a$'s and ends with only $p$. So $L$ is not regular.

**Contrast — a language you cannot kill this way.** $L = \{c^{i}a^{j}b^{k} : i,j,k \ge 0 \text{ and } (i = 1 \Rightarrow j = k)\}$ is **not** regular, yet it satisfies the pumping lemma with $p = 2$: any long string starting with $c^{0}$ or with $c^{2}c\ldots$ can have a symbol in the first two positions pumped without ever having to satisfy $j=k$, and a string starting with exactly one $c$ can pump that $c$ to zero or to two copies, which again escapes the condition. The pumping lemma therefore cannot prove this language non-regular; Myhill-Nerode or a closure argument (intersect with $ca^{*}b^{*}$ to get $\{ca^{n}b^{n}\}$) can. This is the standard demonstration that passing the pumping test proves nothing.

blocks.title: Choosing $w$: push the interesting part past position $p$
blocks.text: The constraint $|xy| \le p$ means the adversary can only touch the **first $p$ symbols**. So design $w$ so that the first $p$ symbols are uniform and the constraint you care about lives after them. For $a^{n}b^{n}$ take $a^{p}b^{p}$, not $a^{p/2}b^{p/2}$; for $\{a^{n}: n \text{ prime}\}$ take $a^{q}$ for a prime $q > p$; for $\{ww\}$ take $a^{p}ba^{p}b$. Done well, the proof has exactly one case.

blocks.q: An NFA has 5 states. The DFA obtained by subset construction has, in the worst case, at most how many states, and is the bound ever attained?
opts: 32 states; attained for suitable languages such as 'the 5th symbol from the end is 1'
blocks.exp: Subset-construction states are subsets of the NFA's state set, so at most $2^{5} = 32$, counting $\varnothing$ as the dead state. The bound is tight: the language whose $k$-th symbol from the end is fixed needs $2^{k}$ DFA states because the DFA must remember the last $k$ symbols, while an NFA guesses the position with $k+1$ states.

blocks.q: A student proves $L = \{a^{n}b^{n}\}$ non-regular as follows: 'Let $p$ be the pumping length. Take $w = a^{p}b^{p}$ and let $y = ab$. Then $xy^{2}z = a^{p+1}b^{p+1}\ldots$'. What is wrong?
opts: $w$ is too short to be pumped
The prover chose the split, but the split is the adversary's move, and $y = ab$ also violates $|xy| \le p$
blocks.exp: You choose only $w$ and $i$; the decomposition $xyz$ is chosen against you, so a proof must cover every legal split. Here the claimed $y = ab$ straddles the block boundary, which $|xy| \le p$ forbids anyway since the first $p$ symbols of $a^{p}b^{p}$ are all $a$'s. The correct argument uses that constraint to show $y$ must be $a^{t}$, then pumps.

blocks.q: Which pair of regular expressions denote **different** languages?
blocks.exp: $a^{*}b^{*}$ contains $aabb$, but every string of $(ab)^{*}$ alternates strictly and has even length with $a$ in every odd position, so $aabb \notin (ab)^{*}$. The others are standard identities: $(r^{*}s^{*})^{*} = (r+s)^{*}$, the shifting law $r(sr)^{*} = (rs)^{*}r$, and the unrolling law $\varepsilon + rr^{*} = r^{*}$.

blocks.q: The minimal DFA for a regular language $L$ over $\{0,1\}$ has 5 states, one of which is a dead state. How many states does the minimal DFA for $\overline{L}$ have?
blocks.exp: Complementation swaps $F$ and $Q-F$ in a complete DFA and changes nothing else, so the state set and transitions are identical and the result is still minimal — if two states were now equivalent they would have been equivalent before, since distinguishability is preserved under swapping acceptance. Hence $\overline{L}$ also needs 5 states; the old dead state simply becomes an accepting sink.

tricks.title: Generate subsets lazily, and count only reachable ones
tricks.body: Never draw all $2^{n}$ subsets. Start from $\text{ECLOSE}(q_0)$ and expand a worklist. Exam answers for 'number of states in the equivalent DFA' mean reachable states; the $2^n$ figure is only the upper bound. Remember $\varnothing$ counts as one state if it is reachable.

tricks.title: Minimisation: delete unreachable states BEFORE table filling
tricks.body: Table filling happily merges unreachable states with reachable ones and gives you a state count that is too high. Reachability first, dead state added second, table third. This one ordering fixes most wrong answers on minimisation numericals.

tricks.title: First marking pass: group states by where they go on each symbol
tricks.body: Instead of scanning pairs one at a time, for each input symbol list which states move into an already-marked class. Any pair that splits that list gets marked. On an 8-state DFA this collapses the first pass to two lines of work.

tricks.title: Product automaton state count is a free answer
tricks.body: For $L_1 \cap L_2$ or $L_1 \cup L_2$ built by the product construction, the answer is $|Q_1| \times |Q_2|$ states before minimisation — accept sets differ ($F_1 \times F_2$ for intersection, $(F_1\times Q_2)\cup(Q_1\times F_2)$ for union) but the state count does not.

tricks.title: To disprove regularity, try closure before the pumping lemma
tricks.body: Intersecting with a simple regular language is usually a one-line proof. $\{w : \#_a = \#_b\} \cap a^{*}b^{*} = \{a^nb^n\}$; $\{ww\} \cap a^{*}ba^{*}b = \{a^nba^nb\}$. Reserve the pumping lemma for when no such reduction is obvious.

traps.title: The pumping lemma cannot prove a language regular
traps.body: It is a one-way implication. Every regular language pumps, but some non-regular languages pump too, such as $\{c^{i}a^{j}b^{k} : i=1 \Rightarrow j=k\}$. If a question asks you to *prove regularity*, build a DFA or a regular expression, or count Myhill-Nerode classes — never cite the pumping lemma.

traps.title: You do not choose the decomposition $xyz$
traps.body: Your moves are $w$ and $i$; the adversary's moves are $p$ and the split. A proof that names a specific $y$ and stops is worth no marks. Use $|xy| \le p$ to constrain the split, then handle every case that survives.

traps.title: NFA to DFA never changes the language, only the state count
traps.body: Non-determinism is not extra power, and neither are $\varepsilon$-moves. Any question claiming NFAs accept a strictly larger class is wrong. The genuine difference is succinctness — up to an exponential blow-up in states, and an $O(2^n)$ conversion cost.

traps.title: A DFA drawn with a missing arrow is incomplete
traps.body: If a transition table has a blank, the machine is not yet a DFA and its state count for minimisation or complementation questions is one higher than drawn. Complementing an incomplete DFA by swapping final states gives the wrong language, because strings that fell off the edge must end up accepted.

traps.title: Linear is not the same as regular
traps.body: $A \to aAb \mid \varepsilon$ has one variable per production and is linear, but generates $a^{n}b^{n}$ and is not regular. Regular grammars additionally require the variable to sit at a consistent end with only terminals on the other side; mixing left-linear and right-linear rules in the same grammar also breaks the guarantee.

topics.title: Context Free Languages, PDA and Normal Forms
topics.summary: CFGs, derivations and ambiguity; pushdown automata under both acceptance conditions; grammar simplification, Chomsky and Greibach normal forms; CYK parsing; closure properties and the CFL pumping lemma.

blocks.text:
## What the stack buys you

A finite automaton cannot count without bound, because its memory is one state out of finitely many. Add a **stack** — unbounded, but accessible only at the top — and the machine can remember how many $a$'s it has seen by pushing one marker per $a$, then pop one per $b$. That single addition takes you from regular to **context-free**, the class that describes nested structure: balanced brackets, block structure, arithmetic expressions, and hence essentially all programming-language syntax.

A **context-free grammar** is $G = (V, T, P, S)$ where every production has the shape

$$A \to \alpha, \qquad A \in V, \ \alpha \in (V \cup T)^{*}.$$

The left side is a **single variable** — that is the whole restriction, and it is what "context-free" means: $A$ may be rewritten regardless of what surrounds it. $\alpha$ may be $\varepsilon$, may be longer or shorter than $A$, and may mix terminals and variables freely.

Examples to keep in mind:

- $S \to aSb \mid \varepsilon$ generates $\{a^{n}b^{n} : n \ge 0\}$.
- $S \to aSa \mid bSb \mid a \mid b \mid \varepsilon$ generates all palindromes over $\{a,b\}$.
- $S \to SS \mid (S) \mid \varepsilon$ generates the balanced-parenthesis strings.
- $S \to aSb \mid aSbb \mid \varepsilon$ generates $\{a^{n}b^{m} : n \le m \le 2n\}$.

## Derivations, parse trees and ambiguity

A **derivation** rewrites $S$ step by step until only terminals remain. In a **leftmost derivation** you always expand the leftmost variable of the current sentential form; in a **rightmost derivation**, the rightmost. A **parse tree** has $S$ at the root, a variable at every internal node with its production's right-hand side as its children in order, and the string read off the leaves left to right (its **yield**).

The relationship is exact and worth stating precisely:

- One parse tree corresponds to exactly **one** leftmost derivation and exactly **one** rightmost derivation.
- Different derivation *orders* of the same tree are not different parses.

A grammar is **ambiguous** if some string in its language has two or more distinct parse trees — equivalently two distinct leftmost derivations, equivalently two distinct rightmost derivations. The classic case:

$$E \to E + E \mid E * E \mid \texttt{id}$$

The string $\texttt{id} + \texttt{id} * \texttt{id}$ parses two ways, one grouping the $+$ first and one the $*$ first. The cure is to build precedence and associativity into the grammar with a level per precedence tier:

$$E \to E + T \mid T, \qquad T \to T * F \mid F, \qquad F \to (E) \mid \texttt{id}$$

Left recursion at each level forces left associativity; putting $*$ at the deeper level forces it to bind tighter. This unambiguous grammar generates the same language and is the standard starting point for topic 8.6.

Two distinctions the examiner uses. First, **ambiguity is a property of the grammar, not of the language** — an ambiguous grammar may well have an unambiguous equivalent. Second, some languages have **no** unambiguous grammar at all; these are **inherently ambiguous**, the standard example being

$$L = \{a^{i}b^{j}c^{k} : i = j \text{ or } j = k\},$$

where strings with $i=j=k$ must be derivable both "the $ab$ way" and "the $bc$ way". Every inherently ambiguous language is non-deterministic (has no DPDA), but the converse fails.

## Pushdown automata

A **PDA** is $P = (Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, Z_0, F)$ with $\Gamma$ the stack alphabet, $Z_0$ the initial stack symbol, and

$$\delta : Q \times (\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\}) \times \Gamma \to \text{finite subsets of } Q \times \Gamma^{*}.$$

A move reads an input symbol (or none), pops one stack symbol, and pushes a string back. An **instantaneous description** is $(q, w, \gamma)$: current state, remaining input, current stack with top at the left.

There are **two acceptance conditions**:

- **Acceptance by final state**: $(q_0, w, Z_0) \vdash^{*} (q, \varepsilon, \gamma)$ with $q \in F$, stack contents irrelevant.
- **Acceptance by empty stack**: $(q_0, w, Z_0) \vdash^{*} (q, \varepsilon, \varepsilon)$, final-state set irrelevant (usually written $F = \varnothing$).

For **non-deterministic** PDAs the two are equivalent in power: from a final-state PDA build an empty-stack one by adding a bottom marker $X_0$ and a state that pops everything once a final state is reached, and vice versa. So $N(P)$ and $L(P)$ range over the same class, which is exactly the context-free languages: **a language is context-free iff some PDA accepts it.**

For **deterministic** PDAs they are *not* equivalent. A DPDA accepting by empty stack can only accept **prefix-free** languages, because once the stack empties the machine is stuck and no longer-string can be accepted. So empty-stack DPDAs are strictly weaker, and "DCFL" always means *accepted by a DPDA with final states*.

Determinism costs real power here, unlike in the finite-automaton case:

$$\text{DCFL} \subsetneq \text{CFL}.$$

$\{ww^{R} : w \in \{a,b\}^{*}\}$ is context-free but not deterministic — no DPDA can know where the middle is. Similarly $\{a^{n}b^{n}\} \cup \{a^{n}b^{2n}\}$ is a CFL but not a DCFL, while $\{a^{n}b^{n}\}$ and $\{wcw^{R}\}$ (with an explicit centre marker) are deterministic.

blocks.title: Worked example — a PDA for $\{a^{n}b^{n} : n \ge 1\}$, both ways
blocks.text:
**Final-state version.** $Q = \{q_0,q_1,q_2\}$, $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$, $\Gamma=\{A,Z_0\}$, $F=\{q_2\}$.

1. $\delta(q_0, a, Z_0) = \{(q_0, AZ_0)\}$ — push the first $A$.
2. $\delta(q_0, a, A) = \{(q_0, AA)\}$ — push one $A$ per $a$.
3. $\delta(q_0, b, A) = \{(q_1, \varepsilon)\}$ — first $b$: pop and switch to the matching phase.
4. $\delta(q_1, b, A) = \{(q_1, \varepsilon)\}$ — pop one $A$ per further $b$.
5. $\delta(q_1, \varepsilon, Z_0) = \{(q_2, Z_0)\}$ — stack back at the bottom marker: accept.

Trace on $aabb$:

$$(q_0, aabb, Z_0) \vdash (q_0, abb, AZ_0) \vdash (q_0, bb, AAZ_0) \vdash (q_1, b, AZ_0) \vdash (q_1, \varepsilon, Z_0) \vdash (q_2, \varepsilon, Z_0)$$

Accepted, because $q_2 \in F$. On $aab$ the machine halts in $(q_1, \varepsilon, AZ_0)$ — not final — and on $abb$ rule 4 has no $A$ to pop, so it dies. Note this PDA is **deterministic**: at most one move applies at each configuration, and no $\varepsilon$-move competes with a symbol move on the same stack top.

**Empty-stack version.** Delete $q_2$ and replace rule 5 by $\delta(q_1, \varepsilon, Z_0) = \{(q_1, \varepsilon)\}$, which pops the bottom marker. Then $aabb$ ends at $(q_1, \varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ and is accepted with $F = \varnothing$. This works here because $\{a^{n}b^{n}\}$ happens to be prefix-free: no string of the language is a proper prefix of another. For a language such as $a^{*}$, where $a$ is a prefix of $aa$, no *deterministic* empty-stack PDA exists.

## Simplifying a grammar

Before any normal form, strip the grammar. Do the steps **in this order** — the order is examinable because doing it wrong reintroduces what you just removed.

1. **Remove $\varepsilon$-productions.** Compute the **nullable** variables: $A$ is nullable if $A \to \varepsilon$, or $A \to B_1 \cdots B_k$ with every $B_i$ nullable. Then for every production, add all variants obtained by deleting any subset of the nullable occurrences on the right, and delete the $\varepsilon$-productions themselves. (If $\varepsilon \in L(G)$, keep a single $S_0 \to \varepsilon$ with a fresh start symbol.)
2. **Remove unit productions** $A \to B$. Compute the unit pairs $(A,B)$ with $A \Rightarrow^{*} B$ using only unit steps, then for each such pair copy every non-unit production of $B$ onto $A$.
3. **Remove useless symbols**, in two sub-passes, again in order: first delete **non-generating** symbols (those from which no terminal string derives), then delete **unreachable** symbols (those not derivable from $S$ in the grammar that remains). Doing reachability first can leave a generating symbol whose only path used a symbol you later delete.

Removing $\varepsilon$-productions can create new unit productions, which is why $\varepsilon$ comes before units; removing units can create useless symbols, which is why useless symbols come last.

## Chomsky Normal Form

A grammar is in **CNF** if every production has one of the forms

$$A \to BC \quad (B, C \text{ variables}), \qquad A \to a \quad (a \text{ a terminal}),$$

plus optionally $S \to \varepsilon$ with $S$ appearing on no right-hand side. Every CFL has a CNF grammar.

Two consequences used constantly in questions:

- A CNF parse tree is binary, so the derivation of a terminal string $w$ with $|w| = n \ge 1$ takes **exactly $2n - 1$ steps** ($n-1$ applications of $A \to BC$ and $n$ of $A \to a$).
- A CNF parse tree of height $h$ yields a string of length at most $2^{h-1}$ — the fact behind the CFL pumping lemma.

blocks.title: Worked example — converting a grammar to CNF
blocks.text:
$$S \to ASA \mid aB, \qquad A \to B \mid S, \qquad B \to b \mid \varepsilon$$

**Step 0 — new start symbol.** Add $S_0 \to S$ so the start symbol never appears on a right-hand side.

**Step 1 — nullable variables.** $B \to \varepsilon$, so $B$ is nullable. $A \to B$, so $A$ is nullable. Is $S$? Its bodies are $ASA$ (needs $S$ nullable, which is what we are testing) and $aB$ (contains the terminal $a$), so no. $S_0$ is not nullable either.

Delete $B \to \varepsilon$ and add every variant with nullable occurrences dropped:

- $S \to ASA$ gives $ASA$, $SA$, $AS$, $S$.
- $S \to aB$ gives $aB$ and $a$.
- $A \to B$ stays; $A \to S$ stays; $A \to \varepsilon$ is not added because we are deleting $\varepsilon$-rules.

$$S_0 \to S; \quad S \to ASA \mid AS \mid SA \mid S \mid aB \mid a; \quad A \to B \mid S; \quad B \to b$$

**Step 2 — unit productions.** The unit rules are $S_0 \to S$, $S \to S$, $A \to B$, $A \to S$. Drop $S \to S$ outright. Unit pairs: $(S_0,S)$, $(A,B)$, $(A,S)$. Copy the non-unit bodies across:

$$S_0 \to ASA \mid AS \mid SA \mid aB \mid a$$
$$S \to ASA \mid AS \mid SA \mid aB \mid a$$
$$A \to b \mid ASA \mid AS \mid SA \mid aB \mid a$$
$$B \to b$$

**Step 3 — useless symbols.** Every variable generates a terminal string ($B \Rightarrow b$, $S \Rightarrow a$, $A \Rightarrow b$, $S_0 \Rightarrow a$) and every variable is reachable from $S_0$. Nothing to delete.

**Step 4 — isolate terminals in long bodies.** Only $aB$ is affected. Introduce $U \to a$ and rewrite $aB$ as $UB$.

**Step 5 — break bodies longer than two.** Only $ASA$ is affected: introduce $X \to SA$ and rewrite $ASA$ as $AX$.

**Result (CNF):**

$$S_0 \to AX \mid AS \mid SA \mid UB \mid a$$
$$S \to AX \mid AS \mid SA \mid UB \mid a$$
$$A \to AX \mid AS \mid SA \mid UB \mid a \mid b$$
$$B \to b, \qquad U \to a, \qquad X \to SA$$

Every body is now two variables or one terminal. As a check, $|w| = 3$ should take $2(3)-1 = 5$ steps: $S_0 \Rightarrow UB \ldots$ no; take $S_0 \Rightarrow AX \Rightarrow aX \Rightarrow aSA \Rightarrow aaA \Rightarrow aab$ — five steps for the three-symbol string $aab$.

## Greibach Normal Form

A grammar is in **GNF** if every production has the form

$$A \to a\alpha, \qquad a \in T, \ \alpha \in V^{*}$$

— exactly one terminal, at the front, followed by zero or more variables. Every CFL not containing $\varepsilon$ has a GNF grammar (add $S_0 \to \varepsilon$ separately if needed).

Why it matters: each derivation step in GNF emits exactly one terminal, so a string of length $n$ takes **exactly $n$ steps**, and the grammar translates directly into a PDA with a single state that pushes $\alpha$ and consumes $a$. GNF is the grammar-side proof that every CFL has a PDA.

The conversion procedure:

1. Put the grammar in CNF and order the variables $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$.
2. For each $i$ in order, rewrite every production $A_i \to A_j \gamma$ with $j < i$ by substituting all bodies of $A_j$, until every remaining production has $j > i$ or begins with a terminal.
3. Eliminate direct left recursion $A \to A\alpha_1 \mid \cdots \mid \beta_1 \mid \cdots$ by $A \to \beta_k \mid \beta_k Z$ and $Z \to \alpha_k \mid \alpha_k Z$.
4. Back-substitute from $A_n$ down to $A_1$, then fix the new $Z$ variables, so every body starts with a terminal.
5. Replace any terminal that is not in the first position by a fresh variable with a single terminal production.

blocks.title: Worked example — a small GNF conversion
blocks.text:
$$S \to Sa \mid Ab, \qquad A \to a$$

First, what is the language? $S \Rightarrow^{*} Ab\,a^{k} \Rightarrow ab a^{k}$, so $L = \{ab\,a^{k} : k \ge 0\} = ab\,a^{*}$.

**Step 1 — eliminate left recursion.** The rule set is $S \to S\alpha \mid \beta$ with $\alpha = a$ and $\beta = Ab$. The standard replacement gives

$$S \to Ab \mid Ab\,S', \qquad S' \to a \mid a S'.$$

$S'$ is already in GNF. $S$ is not, because its bodies start with the variable $A$.

**Step 2 — substitute $A$.** Using $A \to a$:

$$S \to ab \mid ab\,S'.$$

**Step 3 — remove the interior terminal.** GNF allows only variables after the leading terminal, and $b$ is a terminal. Introduce $B \to b$:

$$S \to aB \mid aB\,S', \qquad S' \to a \mid aS', \qquad B \to b.$$

Every body is now one terminal followed by variables, so the grammar is in GNF. ($A$ has become unreachable and is dropped.)

**Verification by derivation length.** The string $aba$ has length 3 and should take exactly 3 steps: $S \Rightarrow aBS' \Rightarrow abS' \Rightarrow aba$. It does.

## CYK parsing

The **Cocke-Younger-Kasami** algorithm decides membership in a CNF grammar's language in $O(n^{3}|G|)$ time and $O(n^{2})$ space, using dynamic programming over substrings.

Let $w = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ and define $X_{i,j}$ = the set of variables that derive the substring $a_i \cdots a_j$. Then

$$X_{i,i} = \{A : A \to a_i \in P\},$$

$$X_{i,j} = \bigcup_{k=i}^{j-1} \{A : A \to BC \in P,\ B \in X_{i,k},\ C \in X_{k+1,j}\}.$$

Fill in order of increasing substring length. Accept $w$ iff $S \in X_{1,n}$. CYK is the standard answer to "which parsing method works for *any* context-free grammar", since LL and LR methods work only for restricted subclasses.

blocks.title: Worked example — CYK on $baaba$
blocks.text:
Grammar in CNF:

$$S \to AB \mid BC, \quad A \to BA \mid a, \quad B \to CC \mid b, \quad C \to AB \mid a$$

Input $w = b\,a\,a\,b\,a$, so $n = 5$.

**Length 1.** $b$ is produced only by $B$; $a$ is produced by $A$ and by $C$.

$$X_{1,1}=\{B\},\ X_{2,2}=\{A,C\},\ X_{3,3}=\{A,C\},\ X_{4,4}=\{B\},\ X_{5,5}=\{A,C\}$$

**Length 2.** Combine adjacent cells and look up bodies.

- $X_{1,2}$: $\{B\}\{A,C\}$ gives $BA$ (so $A$) and $BC$ (so $S$) $\Rightarrow \{S,A\}$.
- $X_{2,3}$: $\{A,C\}\{A,C\}$ gives $AA, AC, CA, CC$; only $CC$ is a body, of $B$ $\Rightarrow \{B\}$.
- $X_{3,4}$: $\{A,C\}\{B\}$ gives $AB$ (bodies of $S$ and $C$) and $CB$ (none) $\Rightarrow \{S,C\}$.
- $X_{4,5}$: $\{B\}\{A,C\}$ $\Rightarrow \{S,A\}$ as in $X_{1,2}$.

**Length 3.** Two splits each.

- $X_{1,3}$: $X_{1,1}X_{2,3} = \{B\}\{B\} = BB$ (none); $X_{1,2}X_{3,3} = \{S,A\}\{A,C\}$ gives $SA, SC, AA, AC$ (none) $\Rightarrow \varnothing$.
- $X_{2,4}$: $X_{2,2}X_{3,4} = \{A,C\}\{S,C\}$ gives $AS,AC,CS,CC$; $CC$ is a body of $B$; $X_{2,3}X_{4,4} = \{B\}\{B\}$ (none) $\Rightarrow \{B\}$.
- $X_{3,5}$: $X_{3,3}X_{4,5} = \{A,C\}\{S,A\}$ (none); $X_{3,4}X_{5,5} = \{S,C\}\{A,C\}$ gives $CC \Rightarrow B$ $\Rightarrow \{B\}$.

**Length 4.**

- $X_{1,4}$: $\{B\}\{B\}$; $\{S,A\}\{S,C\}$; $\varnothing\{B\}$ $\Rightarrow \varnothing$.
- $X_{2,5}$: $X_{2,2}X_{3,5} = \{A,C\}\{B\}$ gives $AB \Rightarrow S, C$; $X_{2,3}X_{4,5} = \{B\}\{S,A\}$ gives $BA \Rightarrow A$; $X_{2,4}X_{5,5} = \{B\}\{A,C\}$ gives $BA \Rightarrow A$ and $BC \Rightarrow S$ $\Rightarrow \{S,A,C\}$.

**Length 5.**

- $X_{1,5}$: $X_{1,1}X_{2,5} = \{B\}\{S,A,C\}$ gives $BA \Rightarrow A$, $BC \Rightarrow S$; $X_{1,2}X_{3,5} = \{S,A\}\{B\}$ gives $AB \Rightarrow S, C$; $X_{1,3}X_{4,5} = \varnothing$; $X_{1,4}X_{5,5} = \varnothing$ $\Rightarrow \{S,A,C\}$.

$S \in X_{1,5}$, so **$baaba$ is in the language**. The full table:

| length | cells |
|---|---|
| 5 | $\{S,A,C\}$ |
| 4 | $\varnothing$, $\{S,A,C\}$ |
| 3 | $\varnothing$, $\{B\}$, $\{B\}$ |
| 2 | $\{S,A\}$, $\{B\}$, $\{S,C\}$, $\{S,A\}$ |
| 1 | $\{B\}$, $\{A,C\}$, $\{A,C\}$, $\{B\}$, $\{A,C\}$ |

## Closure properties

| Operation | CFL | DCFL |
|---|---|---|
| Union | closed | **not** closed |
| Intersection | **not** closed | **not** closed |
| Complement | **not** closed | **closed** |
| Difference | not closed | not closed |
| Intersection with a regular language | **closed** | **closed** |
| Concatenation | closed | not closed |
| Kleene star | closed | not closed |
| Reversal | closed | **not** closed |
| Homomorphism | closed | not closed |
| Inverse homomorphism | closed | closed |
| Substitution | closed | not closed |

The counterexamples worth remembering: $L_1 = \{a^{n}b^{n}c^{m}\}$ and $L_2 = \{a^{m}b^{n}c^{n}\}$ are both context-free, but $L_1 \cap L_2 = \{a^{n}b^{n}c^{n}\}$ is not. Complement then fails automatically, since closure under complement plus closure under union would force closure under intersection via De Morgan.

The DCFL row is the mirror image, and its logic is worth understanding: a DPDA can be complemented (carefully — you must handle configurations where it loops without reading input), which is why DCFLs are closed under complement; but you cannot run two DPDAs at once for a union, because after the first commits to a guess it cannot backtrack.

**Intersection with a regular language** is closed for both, by running the PDA and the DFA in parallel on a product state set. This is the single most useful closure fact in the unit: it converts many "is this a CFL?" questions into a known non-CFL.

## The pumping lemma for context-free languages

**Statement.** If $L$ is context-free, there is a constant $p$ such that every $w \in L$ with $|w| \ge p$ can be written $w = uvxyz$ with

1. $|vxy| \le p$,
2. $|vy| \ge 1$ (so $v$ and $y$ are not both empty),
3. $uv^{i}xy^{i}z \in L$ for every $i \ge 0$.

The proof: in a CNF grammar with $|V| = m$ variables, take $p = 2^{m}$. A string of length $\ge p$ needs a parse tree of height $> m$, so some root-to-leaf path repeats a variable $A$; the subtree at the upper $A$ yields $vxy$ and the subtree at the lower $A$ yields $x$, and you may splice the upper subtree into itself any number of times. Because $v$ and $y$ grow **together**, this lemma pumps **two** places at once — that is exactly the difference from the regular version, and it is why three independent counts defeat it.

The adversary game is identical to topic 8.2: the adversary picks $p$, you pick $w$, the adversary picks the decomposition subject to $|vxy| \le p$ and $|vy| \ge 1$, you pick $i$. Once again you may **not** choose the split, and the lemma can never prove a language *is* context-free.

For the few languages where the plain lemma is too weak, **Ogden's lemma** strengthens it by letting you mark $p$ positions and forcing $v$ and $y$ to contain marked ones — useful for proving inherent ambiguity, but rarely needed at this level.

blocks.title: Worked example — $\{a^{n}b^{n}c^{n}\}$ is not context-free
blocks.text:
Let the adversary supply $p$. Choose $w = a^{p}b^{p}c^{p}$, which is in $L$ and has length $3p \ge p$.

The adversary writes $w = uvxyz$ with $|vxy| \le p$ and $|vy| \ge 1$. Since $vxy$ is a window of length at most $p$ inside a string whose three blocks each have length $p$, that window **cannot touch both the $a$-block and the $c$-block** — they are $p$ symbols apart. So exactly one of these holds:

- **Case 1: $vxy$ lies within $a^{p}b^{p}$.** Then $c$'s are never pumped. Take $i = 2$: $uv^{2}xy^{2}z$ has more than $p$ symbols among $a$ and $b$ combined (since $|vy| \ge 1$) but still exactly $p$ $c$'s. The three counts can no longer all be equal, so the string leaves $L$.
- **Case 2: $vxy$ lies within $b^{p}c^{p}$.** Symmetrically, $a$'s are never pumped, the count of $a$'s stays at $p$ while the $b$/$c$ total grows, and again the string leaves $L$.

Every legal split falls into one of the two cases and fails, so $L$ is not context-free.

**A second one — $L = \{ww : w \in \{a,b\}^{*}\}$ is not context-free.** Given $p$, choose $w = a^{p}b^{p}a^{p}b^{p}$. Take any split with $|vxy| \le p$; the window sits inside at most two adjacent blocks, so pumping to $i=2$ changes the count of one symbol in one half without making the matching change in the other half, and the result is no longer of the form $ss$. (Choosing the naive $a^{p}b^{p}$ here fails: it *is* pumpable as $ss$ with $s = a^{p/2}b^{p/2}$-style splits, which is why the four-block string is the standard choice.)

**Contrast.** $\{a^{n}b^{n}c^{m}\}$ *is* context-free — only two counts are tied, and a stack handles two. The rule of thumb: one stack matches one pair of counts. Three simultaneous equalities, or two *crossing* dependencies as in $\{a^{i}b^{j}c^{i}d^{j}\}$, are beyond a PDA.

blocks.q: A grammar is in Chomsky Normal Form. How many derivation steps are needed to derive a terminal string of length 8?
blocks.exp: Each $A \to BC$ step increases the number of variables in the sentential form by one, and each $A \to a$ step converts one variable to one terminal. Starting from a single variable and ending with 8 terminals needs $8-1 = 7$ binary steps and 8 terminal steps, so $2n-1 = 15$ in total, whatever the CNF grammar is.

blocks.q: Which of the following is context-free but **not** deterministic context-free?
blocks.exp: Even-length palindromes are generated by $S \to aSa \mid bSb \mid \varepsilon$, so they are context-free, but a deterministic machine has no way to detect the midpoint and must guess — hence no DPDA. With an explicit centre marker $c$ the guess disappears and $\{wcw^{R}\}$ is deterministic; $\{a^{n}b^{n}\}$ is deterministic; $\{a^{n}b^{n}c^{n}\}$ is not context-free at all.

blocks.q: $L_1$ is context-free and $L_2$ is regular. Which statement is guaranteed?
opts: $L_1 \cap L_2$ may fail to be context-free
blocks.exp: Run the PDA for $L_1$ and the DFA for $L_2$ simultaneously on the product state set, keeping the single stack; the result is a PDA, so CFLs are closed under intersection with a regular language. It need not be regular ($\{a^nb^n\} \cap a^{*}b^{*}$ is still non-regular), and CFLs are not closed under complement, so option 3 fails.

blocks.q: In the CYK table for a string of length $n$, which entry decides membership, and what is the running time?
blocks.exp: $X_{1,n}$ holds the variables deriving the whole string, so the string is accepted iff the start symbol is in it. There are $O(n^{2})$ cells and each is filled by trying $O(n)$ split points, giving $O(n^{3})$ time (times the grammar size), with $O(n^{2})$ space.

tricks.title: CNF step count is a one-line answer
tricks.body: $|w| = n$ needs exactly $2n-1$ steps in CNF and exactly $n$ steps in GNF. Questions asking 'how many productions are applied' never need the grammar at all — only the normal form and the string length.

tricks.title: Count the tied quantities to decide CFL or not
tricks.body: One stack tracks one matching pair. $\{a^nb^nc^m\}$ and $\{a^nb^mc^m\}$: context-free. $\{a^nb^nc^n\}$ (three tied) and $\{a^ib^jc^id^j\}$ (crossing pairs): not. Nesting is fine, crossing is not.

tricks.title: For 'is it a CFL?' questions, intersect with a regular language
tricks.body: CFLs are closed under intersection with regular sets, so if $L \cap R$ is a known non-CFL for some simple regular $R$, then $L$ is not a CFL. This is faster and less error-prone than a pumping argument.

tricks.title: Simplify in the fixed order: $\varepsilon$, then units, then useless
tricks.body: Removing $\varepsilon$-rules creates unit rules; removing unit rules creates useless symbols. Going the other way forces you to repeat passes. Within the useless-symbol step, non-generating symbols go before unreachable ones.

tricks.title: Pick four blocks, not two, when pumping $\{ww\}$
tricks.body: $a^{p}b^{p}$ survives the CFL pumping lemma as a member of $\{ww\}$-like sets; $a^{p}b^{p}a^{p}b^{p}$ does not, because the length-$p$ window $vxy$ cannot reach the corresponding position in the other half. Choosing $w$ so that the window is too short to keep two halves in step is the whole art.

traps.title: Ambiguity belongs to grammars; inherent ambiguity belongs to languages
traps.body: '$G$ is ambiguous' says nothing about $L(G)$ — the standard expression grammar has an unambiguous equivalent. Only when *every* grammar for the language is ambiguous is the language inherently ambiguous, e.g. $\{a^ib^jc^k : i=j \text{ or } j=k\}$. Also: checking whether a given CFG is ambiguous is undecidable.

traps.title: Empty-stack and final-state acceptance differ for DPDAs only
traps.body: For non-deterministic PDAs the two conditions define the same class. For deterministic ones, empty-stack acceptance can only give prefix-free languages, so 'DCFL' means final-state acceptance. A question contrasting the two is testing exactly this asymmetry.

traps.title: CFLs are not closed under intersection or complement
traps.body: This is the most exploited closure fact in the unit. $\{a^nb^nc^m\} \cap \{a^mb^nc^n\} = \{a^nb^nc^n\}$ is the counterexample to memorise. Regular languages are closed under everything; CFLs are not; DCFLs swap the pattern by being closed under complement but not union.

traps.title: The CFL pumping lemma pumps $v$ and $y$ together
traps.body: You cannot pump one of them and freeze the other — the exponent $i$ is shared. This is why it defeats $\{a^nb^nc^n\}$ (two of the three blocks would have to grow, breaking equality with the third) but does not defeat $\{a^nb^n\}$, which is context-free precisely because $v$ and $y$ can sit in the two matching blocks.

topics.title: Turing Machines and the Chomsky Hierarchy
topics.summary: Turing machines and their equivalent variants, the Church-Turing thesis, recursive versus recursively enumerable languages and their differing closure properties, linear bounded automata and context-sensitive languages, and the complete Chomsky hierarchy.

blocks.text:
## The machine that finishes the ladder

A finite automaton has no memory beyond its state; a PDA has a stack, which it can only read at the top; a Turing machine has an **unbounded tape it can both read and write at any position**. That is the last upgrade needed — no further addition of resources changes what is computable, only how fast.

A (deterministic, one-tape) **Turing machine** is $M = (Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, B, F)$ with $\Sigma \subseteq \Gamma$ the input alphabet, $\Gamma$ the tape alphabet, $B \in \Gamma \setminus \Sigma$ the blank symbol, and

$$\delta : Q \times \Gamma \to Q \times \Gamma \times \{L, R\}.$$

One move reads the scanned symbol, writes a symbol in its place, moves the head one cell left or right, and changes state. A **configuration** (instantaneous description) is written $\alpha q \beta$: the tape contents left of the head, the current state, and the tape from the head rightwards, with trailing blanks omitted.

There are two ways for a machine to fail to accept, and keeping them apart is the whole of computability theory:

- it can **halt** in a non-accepting state — a definite "no";
- it can **loop forever** — no answer at all.

$M$ **accepts** $w$ if some computation from $q_0 w$ reaches an accepting state. $L(M)$ is the set of accepted strings. $M$ is a **decider** if it halts on every input, accepting or rejecting.

blocks.title: Worked example — a Turing machine for $\{a^{n}b^{n} : n \ge 0\}$, with a full trace
blocks.text:
Idea: repeatedly cross off the leftmost unmatched $a$ (write $X$), run right to the leftmost unmatched $b$ (write $Y$), run back, and repeat. Accept when no $a$'s remain and nothing but $Y$'s follow.

$\Gamma = \{a, b, X, Y, B\}$, $F = \{q_4\}$.

| state | $a$ | $b$ | $X$ | $Y$ | $B$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $q_0$ | $(q_1, X, R)$ | — | — | $(q_3, Y, R)$ | $(q_4, B, R)$ |
| $q_1$ | $(q_1, a, R)$ | $(q_2, Y, L)$ | — | $(q_1, Y, R)$ | — |
| $q_2$ | $(q_2, a, L)$ | — | $(q_0, X, R)$ | $(q_2, Y, L)$ | — |
| $q_3$ | — | — | — | $(q_3, Y, R)$ | $(q_4, B, R)$ |
| $q_4$ | accept | | | | |

$q_0$ looks at the leftmost unprocessed cell, $q_1$ scans right for a $b$, $q_2$ scans back left to the last $X$, and $q_3$ verifies that only $Y$'s remain.

**Trace on $aabb$** (the head position is marked by the state symbol immediately to its left):

$$q_0aabb \vdash Xq_1abb \vdash Xaq_1bb \vdash Xq_2aYb \vdash q_2XaYb \vdash Xq_0aYb$$
$$\vdash XXq_1Yb \vdash XXYq_1b \vdash XXq_2YY \vdash Xq_2XYY \vdash XXq_0YY$$
$$\vdash XXYq_3Y \vdash XXYYq_3B \vdash XXYYBq_4$$

Thirteen moves, ending in $q_4$: **accepted**.

**Trace on $aab$** (short by one $b$): after matching one pair the machine reaches $Xq_0aYB$ — wait, more carefully, it reaches $XXq_1Y$ then $XXYq_1B$, and $\delta(q_1, B)$ is undefined, so the machine **halts and rejects**. On $abb$ the run is $q_0abb \vdash Xq_1bb \vdash q_2XYb \vdash Xq_0Yb \vdash XYq_3b$, and $\delta(q_3, b)$ is undefined, so again it halts and rejects. Because every undefined entry is a halt, this machine is a **decider**: it halts on every input, which is what makes $\{a^{n}b^{n}\}$ recursive as well as context-free.

## Variants, and why none of them matter

Every one of the following accepts exactly the recursively enumerable languages — the *equivalence* is what is examined, and the *cost* of simulation is the follow-up question:

| Variant | Simulation cost |
|---|---|
| Two-way infinite tape | none (fold the tape into two tracks) |
| Multi-track tape | none (tape alphabet becomes $\Gamma^{k}$) |
| $k$-tape machine | one-tape simulation in $O(t^{2})$ time for $t$ steps |
| Multi-head, single tape | as multi-tape |
| Two-dimensional tape | polynomial slowdown |
| Non-deterministic TM | deterministic simulation in $2^{O(t)}$ time (breadth-first over the computation tree) |
| Machine with a "stay" option | none |
| Machine that never writes | *weaker* — it is just a two-way finite automaton, hence regular |
| Two-counter machine | equivalent to a TM (Minsky); a **one**-counter machine is strictly weaker |

Two points examiners like. First, non-determinism does not add power to Turing machines — it adds at most an exponential speed-up, and whether that speed-up is real is the P vs NP question. Second, the direction of the simulation matters for the language class only if some *resource* is bounded; an LBA, below, is exactly a TM with a bounded tape, and there the restriction does bite.

A **universal Turing machine** $U$ takes an encoded machine and input $\langle M, w \rangle$ and simulates $M$ on $w$. Its existence is the theoretical statement that a stored-program computer is possible, and it is the object on which all the undecidability proofs of topic 8.5 operate.

The **Church-Turing thesis** asserts that every function computable by any effective mechanical procedure is computable by a Turing machine. It is a *thesis*, not a theorem — it identifies an informal notion (algorithm) with a formal one (TM), so it cannot be proved, only supported. Its support is that $\lambda$-calculus, general recursive functions, Post systems, register machines, and every programming language ever defined have turned out to compute exactly the same functions.

## Recursive and recursively enumerable

Two classes, and the difference is *halting*, not *accepting*:

- $L$ is **recursively enumerable (RE)**, or Turing-recognisable, if some TM accepts exactly the strings of $L$. On a string not in $L$ it may reject or may loop forever.
- $L$ is **recursive**, or decidable, if some TM accepts exactly $L$ **and halts on every input**. A decider always answers.

Clearly recursive $\subseteq$ RE, and the containment is strict: the halting language $L_{u} = \{\langle M, w\rangle : M \text{ accepts } w\}$ is RE (simulate) but not recursive.

The single most useful theorem about these classes:

**If $L$ and $\overline{L}$ are both RE, then $L$ is recursive.**

Proof sketch (dovetailing): run the recogniser for $L$ and the recogniser for $\overline{L}$ in parallel, one step each alternately. Every string lies in $L$ or in $\overline{L}$, so one of them accepts after finitely many steps; report accordingly and halt. Contrapositive, used constantly: if $L$ is RE but not recursive, then $\overline{L}$ is **not even RE**. That is why $\overline{L_{u}}$ — the set of $\langle M,w\rangle$ with $M$ not accepting $w$ — is non-RE.

The name "recursively enumerable" is literal: $L$ is RE iff some TM can *list* its members, printing them one after another (in no particular order, possibly with repetitions). $L$ is recursive iff some TM can list them **in shortlex order**, because only then does failure to appear become detectable.

## Closure properties: where the two classes differ

| Operation | Recursive | Recursively enumerable |
|---|---|---|
| Union | closed | closed |
| Intersection | closed | closed |
| **Complement** | **closed** | **NOT closed** |
| Difference $L_1 - L_2$ | closed | **NOT closed** |
| Concatenation | closed | closed |
| Kleene star | closed | closed |
| Reversal | closed | closed |
| Homomorphism | **NOT closed** | closed |
| Inverse homomorphism | closed | closed |
| Intersection with a regular language | closed | closed |

Two rows carry all the exam weight.

**Complement.** Recursive languages are closed under complement because you can swap accept and reject on a machine that always halts. RE languages are not, because swapping does nothing about the branch that loops; and if they were closed, the theorem above would make every RE language recursive, collapsing the hierarchy.

**Homomorphism.** RE is closed under homomorphism: to recognise $h(L)$, non-deterministically guess a pre-image and check it — looping forever on a wrong guess is permitted. Recursive languages are *not* closed under homomorphism, precisely because that guess cannot be bounded, so the guessing machine may not halt. This is the one row students routinely get backwards: RE is the more permissive class for homomorphism, the less permissive for complement.

## Linear bounded automata and context-sensitive languages

A **linear bounded automaton** is a non-deterministic Turing machine restricted to the tape cells occupied by its input (bounded by end markers, or equivalently by $cn$ cells for a constant $c$ — hence "linear bounded"). Its languages are exactly the **context-sensitive languages**.

Because the tape is bounded, the number of distinct configurations is finite:

$$|Q| \times n \times |\Gamma|^{n},$$

states times head positions times tape contents. A computation longer than that must repeat a configuration and hence loop, so a simulator can cut it off. Therefore **every context-sensitive language is recursive** — and the containment is strict, since a diagonal argument produces recursive languages outside CSL.

A **context-sensitive grammar** has productions

$$\alpha A \beta \to \alpha \gamma \beta, \qquad \gamma \ne \varepsilon,$$

— a variable may be rewritten only *in the context* $\alpha \ldots \beta$. Equivalently (and more usefully for checking a grammar) every production $\alpha \to \beta$ satisfies $|\alpha| \le |\beta|$; such grammars are called **non-contracting** or monotonic. The single exception is $S \to \varepsilon$, allowed if $S$ never appears on a right-hand side, so that $\varepsilon$ can be in the language.

Non-contraction is what makes membership decidable: since sentential forms never shrink, deriving a string of length $n$ can only pass through strings of length $\le n$, of which there are finitely many, so exhaustive search terminates. CSL membership is decidable but **PSPACE-complete** — decidable is not the same as practical.

The standard example: $\{a^{n}b^{n}c^{n} : n \ge 1\}$ is context-sensitive but not context-free, generated by

$$S \to aSBC \mid aBC, \quad CB \to BC, \quad aB \to ab, \quad bB \to bb, \quad bC \to bc, \quad cC \to cc.$$

An **unrestricted (type-0) grammar** drops all restrictions: $\alpha \to \beta$ with $\alpha$ containing at least one variable, and $\beta$ arbitrary, possibly shorter. Productions may now delete material, the search space becomes unbounded, and the generated languages are exactly the recursively enumerable ones.

## The Chomsky hierarchy, complete

| Type | Grammar | Production form | Machine | Language class | Membership |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **3** | Regular | $A \to aB$, $A \to a$ (or all left-linear) | Finite automaton (DFA = NFA) | Regular | $O(n)$ |
| **2** | Context-free | $A \to \alpha$, $\alpha \in (V\cup T)^{*}$ | Pushdown automaton (non-det.) | Context-free | $O(n^{3})$ (CYK) |
| **1** | Context-sensitive | $\alpha A \beta \to \alpha\gamma\beta$, $\gamma \ne \varepsilon$; equivalently $\lvert\alpha\rvert \le \lvert\beta\rvert$ | Linear bounded automaton | Context-sensitive | decidable, PSPACE-complete |
| **0** | Unrestricted | $\alpha \to \beta$, $\alpha$ contains a variable | Turing machine | Recursively enumerable | undecidable |

The strict containments are

$$\text{Regular} \subsetneq \text{DCFL} \subsetneq \text{CFL} \subsetneq \text{CSL} \subsetneq \text{Recursive} \subsetneq \text{RE} \subsetneq \text{all languages}.$$

Note that **recursive** has no type number and no grammar of its own — it sits strictly between type 1 and type 0, and the machine characterisation is "Turing machine that always halts". Questions that ask "which grammar generates exactly the recursive languages?" have the answer **none of the four types**; that is the point of the gap.

Separating examples, one per gap, worth memorising as a chain:

- regular but not finite: $a^{*}$
- DCFL but not regular: $\{a^{n}b^{n}\}$
- CFL but not DCFL: $\{ww^{R}\}$
- CSL but not CFL: $\{a^{n}b^{n}c^{n}\}$, $\{ww\}$, $\{a^{p} : p \text{ prime}\}$
- recursive but not CSL: a language built by diagonalising over LBAs
- RE but not recursive: $L_{u}$, the universal/halting language
- not even RE: $\overline{L_{u}}$, and the diagonal language $L_{d}$

blocks.title: Deciders, recognisers and the word 'semi-decidable'
blocks.text:
Three phrases for the same idea, and they appear interchangeably in question papers:

- **Decidable = recursive = Turing-decidable**: a TM that halts on all inputs.
- **Semi-decidable = recursively enumerable = Turing-recognisable = partially decidable**: a TM that halts on all *yes*-instances.
- **Turing-acceptable** is another synonym for RE.

So "is $L$ semi-decidable?" and "is $L$ recursively enumerable?" are the same question. A language that is semi-decidable and whose complement is also semi-decidable is decidable.

blocks.q: $L$ is recursively enumerable but not recursive. What can be said about $\overline{L}$?
opts: $\overline{L}$ is recursively enumerable but not recursive
