blocks.exp: If both $L$ and $\overline{L}$ were RE, running their two recognisers in parallel would decide $L$, making it recursive — contradicting the premise. So $\overline{L}$ cannot be RE at all. This is the standard route to exhibiting non-RE languages, e.g. $\overline{L_{u}}$.

blocks.q: Which class is **not** closed under complementation?
blocks.exp: Regular languages complement by swapping final states in a complete DFA; recursive languages by swapping accept and reject on a halting machine; context-sensitive languages by the Immerman-Szelepcsenyi theorem on non-deterministic space. Context-free languages fail: $\{a^{n}b^{n}c^{m}\}$ and $\{a^{m}b^{n}c^{n}\}$ are CFLs whose intersection is not, and closure under complement plus union would force closure under intersection.

blocks.q: A linear bounded automaton with $|Q|$ states, tape alphabet $\Gamma$ and input of length $n$ has how many distinct configurations, and what does that imply?
opts: $|Q| \cdot n \cdot |\Gamma|^{n}$; the number is finite, so looping is detectable and every CSL is recursive
infinitely many; CSL membership is undecidable
$|Q| + n + |\Gamma|$; CSL membership is linear time
blocks.exp: A configuration is a state, a head position among $n$ cells, and the contents of those $n$ cells, giving $|Q| \cdot n \cdot |\Gamma|^{n}$ possibilities. Any computation longer than that repeats a configuration and therefore loops forever, so a simulator can impose that bound and always halt. Hence CSL $\subseteq$ recursive, though the bound is exponential, and membership is PSPACE-complete.

blocks.q: Which statement about the Church-Turing thesis is correct?
opts: It is a theorem proved by Turing in 1936
It states that no problem is undecidable
It is an unprovable claim identifying 'effectively computable' with 'Turing computable', supported by the equivalence of many independent models
It states that non-deterministic Turing machines are more powerful than deterministic ones
blocks.exp: The thesis equates an informal notion (what a mechanical procedure can compute) with a precise one (what a TM computes). Because one side is informal, it cannot be proved; its evidence is that lambda-calculus, general recursive functions, Post systems, register machines and every real programming language define exactly the same class of computable functions.

tricks.title: Recursive means 'halts always'; RE means 'halts on yes'
tricks.body: Translate every statement into this one difference before reasoning. 'Accepts $L$' alone never implies decidability; the extra clause 'and halts on every input' is the whole content of recursiveness, and questions often hide it or leave it out deliberately.

tricks.title: $L$ and $\overline{L}$ both RE $\Rightarrow$ recursive — use it in both directions
tricks.body: Forwards it decides languages; backwards (contrapositive) it produces non-RE languages from RE-but-undecidable ones. Almost every question asking 'which of these is not RE?' is answered by spotting the complement of a known undecidable problem.

tricks.title: Two closure rows differ; memorise only those
tricks.body: Recursive and RE agree on union, intersection, concatenation, star, reversal and inverse homomorphism. They differ on **complement** (recursive yes, RE no) and **homomorphism** (RE yes, recursive no). Learning those two exceptions beats learning two full tables.

tricks.title: Check a grammar's type by the shortest rule that breaks it
tricks.body: Scan for one production that violates the stricter class. A single $\alpha \to \beta$ with $|\alpha| > |\beta|$ drops the grammar to type 0; a single body with two variables in a right-linear grammar drops it to type 2; two symbols on the left drops it below type 2. The type is decided by the worst production, not the majority.

tricks.title: Separating examples as a memorised chain
tricks.body: $a^{*}$ (regular) $\to \{a^nb^n\}$ (DCFL) $\to \{ww^R\}$ (CFL) $\to \{a^nb^nc^n\}$ (CSL) $\to L_u$ (RE) $\to \overline{L_u}$ (non-RE). Any 'which class does this belong to' question is answered by matching the given language to the nearest link in the chain.

traps.title: Non-determinism adds power to PDAs but not to TMs or FAs
traps.body: NFA $=$ DFA, NTM $=$ DTM (in power), but NPDA $\supsetneq$ DPDA. Two of the three models collapse and one does not, and questions deliberately mix the three. The LBA definition is non-deterministic by convention, and whether deterministic LBAs are equally powerful is still open.

traps.title: Recursive languages have no Chomsky type
traps.body: The four types are regular, context-free, context-sensitive and recursively enumerable. Recursive sits strictly between types 1 and 0 and corresponds to no grammar restriction — it is defined by a machine property (always halts), not a production shape.

traps.title: Context-sensitive means non-contracting, not 'has context on both sides'
traps.body: The practical test is $|\alpha| \le |\beta|$ for every production. A rule like $AB \to BA$ is context-sensitive by that test even though it looks like a swap rather than a contextual rewrite; a rule like $AB \to A$ is not, because it shortens.

traps.title: RE is closed under homomorphism; recursive is not
traps.body: The intuition 'recursive is the better-behaved class, so it must be closed under more operations' is wrong here. Guessing a pre-image is fine for a recogniser that may loop, but a decider cannot bound the guess, so the image of a recursive language under a homomorphism may be merely RE.

topics.title: Unsolvable Problems and Computational Complexity
topics.summary: The halting problem and its proof, reductions, Rice's theorem, the Post correspondence problem, the decidable and undecidable questions about grammars, and the complexity classes P, NP, NP-complete and beyond.

blocks.text:
## The halting problem

The counting argument of topic 8.1 guarantees that undecidable languages exist. The halting problem is the first concrete one, and it is undecidable by self-reference rather than by counting.

Define

$$\text{HALT} = \{\langle M, w\rangle : \text{TM } M \text{ halts on input } w\}.$$

**Theorem.** HALT is undecidable.

**Proof.** Suppose a decider $H$ exists: $H(\langle M, w\rangle)$ halts and outputs "yes" if $M$ halts on $w$ and "no" otherwise. Build a new machine $D$ that takes one input $\langle M \rangle$ and does this:

```
D(<M>):
    run H(<M>, <M>)
    if H says "halts":  loop forever
    if H says "loops":  halt
```

Now run $D$ on its own description $\langle D \rangle$.

- If $D$ halts on $\langle D \rangle$, then $H(\langle D\rangle,\langle D\rangle)$ said "halts", so $D$ was built to loop forever — contradiction.
- If $D$ loops on $\langle D \rangle$, then $H$ said "loops", so $D$ was built to halt — contradiction.

Both branches are impossible, so $H$ cannot exist. This is Russell's paradox and Cantor's diagonal in machine form: $D$ is engineered to disagree with the diagonal entry of the table "does machine $i$ halt on input $i$".

Note what is and is not being claimed. HALT is **recursively enumerable** — simulate $M$ on $w$ and accept if the simulation stops — but not recursive, because there is no point at which you may safely give up. Consequently $\overline{\text{HALT}}$ is **not even RE**. And the theorem says no *single* algorithm works for all pairs; for a particular program you may well be able to prove termination by hand.

## Reductions: the workhorse

Almost no undecidability proof after the first uses diagonalisation directly; they all use **reduction**.

A **mapping (many-one) reduction** $A \le_m B$ is a computable total function $f$ with

$$x \in A \iff f(x) \in B.$$

The two consequences, and their directions, are everything:

- If $A \le_m B$ and $B$ is decidable, then $A$ is decidable. (Solve $A$ by translating and calling $B$'s decider.)
- Contrapositive: if $A \le_m B$ and $A$ is **un**decidable, then $B$ is undecidable.

So to prove a new problem $B$ undecidable, reduce a **known** undecidable problem $A$ **to** $B$ — the known one is the *source*. Getting this backwards ("I reduced my problem to the halting problem, therefore it is undecidable") proves nothing, since reducing to an undecidable problem is trivially possible and says nothing about the source.

The same machinery, with the reduction required to run in polynomial time, gives NP-hardness later in this topic: identical direction, different resource bound.

blocks.title: Worked example — emptiness of $L(M)$ is undecidable
blocks.text:
Let $E_{TM} = \{\langle M\rangle : L(M) = \varnothing\}$. We show $A_{TM} = \{\langle M, w\rangle : M \text{ accepts } w\} \le_m \overline{E_{TM}}$, which suffices because $A_{TM}$ is undecidable.

**The reduction.** Given $\langle M, w\rangle$, construct (do not run) a new machine $M_{w}$:

```
M_w(x):
    if x != w:  reject
    else:       run M on w and accept if M accepts
```

$M_w$ is built by a simple program that just writes out a description, so the construction is computable.

**What is $L(M_w)$?**

- If $M$ accepts $w$, then $M_w$ accepts exactly the one string $w$, so $L(M_w) = \{w\} \ne \varnothing$.
- If $M$ does not accept $w$, then $M_w$ accepts nothing, so $L(M_w) = \varnothing$.

Hence $\langle M, w\rangle \in A_{TM} \iff \langle M_w \rangle \notin E_{TM}$.

**Conclusion.** If $E_{TM}$ were decidable, its decider would decide $A_{TM}$ by negating the answer, contradicting the undecidability of $A_{TM}$. So $E_{TM}$ is undecidable.

**A finer point that questions exploit.** $E_{TM}$ is undecidable and, moreover, **not RE**: the reduction above maps $A_{TM}$ to its *complement*, and $\overline{E_{TM}}$ is the RE one (guess a string, guess a number of steps, verify acceptance). Knowing which of a problem and its complement is RE is often the real question.

## Rice's theorem

Rice's theorem generalises every proof of the shape above in one stroke.

**Statement.** Let $P$ be any **non-trivial property of the language** recognised by a Turing machine — that is, $P$ holds for the language of some TM and fails for the language of some other TM. Then

$$\{\langle M\rangle : L(M) \text{ has property } P\}$$

is **undecidable**.

Two conditions, both of which are where the marks are:

1. **It must be a property of $L(M)$, not of $M$.** If $L(M_1) = L(M_2)$ then either both descriptions have the property or neither does. "The machine has fewer than 10 states", "the machine halts within 100 steps on the empty input", "the machine ever writes the symbol $X$" are properties of the *description* and are perfectly decidable — Rice says nothing about them.
2. **It must be non-trivial.** A property that every RE language has (e.g. "$L(M)$ is recursively enumerable") or that none has is trivially decidable: always answer yes, or always no.

Undecidable by Rice, immediately: $L(M) = \varnothing$; $L(M)$ is finite; $L(M)$ is infinite; $L(M)$ is regular; $L(M)$ is context-free; $L(M) = \Sigma^{*}$; $L(M)$ contains the string $\texttt{hello}$; $|L(M)| = 5$; $L(M) = L(M')$ for a fixed $M'$.

Decidable, and therefore not contradicting Rice: does $M$ have an even number of states; does $M$ move left on its first step; does $M$ halt on $w$ **within $k$ steps** for a given $k$ (just simulate $k$ steps).

## Post's correspondence problem

PCP is the undecidable problem of choice when the target has nothing to do with machines — it is the bridge used to prove grammar problems undecidable.

**Instance.** Two lists of strings over $\Sigma$ of equal length,

$$A = w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_k \qquad B = x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_k.$$

Think of them as $k$ types of domino, the $i$-th having $w_i$ on top and $x_i$ underneath.

**Question.** Is there a non-empty finite sequence of indices $i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_m$ (repetitions allowed) with

$$w_{i_1}w_{i_2}\cdots w_{i_m} = x_{i_1}x_{i_2}\cdots x_{i_m}\,?$$

**Theorem (Post, 1946).** PCP is undecidable. The **modified PCP** (MPCP), which additionally requires the solution to begin with index 1, is undecidable too, and the standard proof goes MPCP $\le$ PCP with a marker-symbol encoding, and computation histories of a TM $\le$ MPCP.

Two special cases are decidable and are worth knowing: PCP with $k = 1$ is trivial, and PCP over a **unary** alphabet is decidable (it reduces to comparing integer ratios). PCP with $k = 2$ is also known to be decidable; undecidability sets in by $k = 5$.

blocks.title: Worked example — solving and refuting PCP instances
blocks.text:
**(a) A solvable instance.**

| $i$ | $w_i$ (top) | $x_i$ (bottom) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $1$ | $111$ |
| 2 | $10111$ | $10$ |
| 3 | $10$ | $0$ |

Try the index sequence $2,1,1,3$:

- Top: $10111 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 10 = 101111110$
- Bottom: $10 \cdot 111 \cdot 111 \cdot 0 = 101111110$

They match (both have length 9), so this instance **has a solution**. Note the first tile must be 2: for tile 1, $1$ versus $111$ — a prefix, fine — but the working shows 2 is what closes; in general you search by keeping track of the current *overhang*, the part by which one side leads.

**(b) An unsolvable instance.**

| $i$ | $w_i$ | $x_i$ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $10$ | $101$ |
| 2 | $011$ | $11$ |
| 3 | $101$ | $011$ |

Any solution starts with a tile whose two strings are prefix-compatible. Tile 2: $011$ vs $11$ — differ at the first symbol, impossible. Tile 3: $101$ vs $011$ — differ at the first symbol, impossible. So the solution must start with **tile 1**, leaving top $= 10$, bottom $= 101$: the bottom leads by the overhang $1$.

With overhang $1$ on the bottom, the next tile must have $w_i$ starting with $1$: tile 1 or tile 3.

- Tile 1: top becomes $1010$, bottom $101101$. Compare position by position: $1,0,1,0$ against $1,0,1,1$ — mismatch at the fourth symbol. Dead.
- Tile 3: top becomes $10101$, bottom $101011$. The first five symbols agree, and the bottom again leads by the overhang $1$.

So the only surviving move returns the configuration to "bottom leads by $1$", which is exactly where we started. The overhang can never be consumed, the two sides never level up, and the instance has **no solution**.

The point of the example is the method: track the overhang as a state, and either reach overhang $\varepsilon$ (solution) or show the reachable overhangs cycle without ever hitting $\varepsilon$.

## What is decidable about grammars

| Question | Regular | DCFL | CFL | CSL / RE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $w \in L$? (membership) | decidable | decidable | decidable (CYK) | decidable for CSL, undecidable for RE |
| $L = \varnothing$? | decidable | decidable | **decidable** | undecidable |
| $L$ finite / infinite? | decidable | decidable | **decidable** | undecidable |
| $L_1 = L_2$? | decidable | decidable | **undecidable** | undecidable |
| $L_1 \subseteq L_2$? | decidable | undecidable | undecidable | undecidable |
| $L_1 \cap L_2 = \varnothing$? | decidable | undecidable | undecidable | undecidable |
| $L = \Sigma^{*}$? | decidable | decidable | **undecidable** | undecidable |
| Is $L$ regular? | trivial | decidable | **undecidable** | undecidable |
| Is $G$ ambiguous? | — | — | **undecidable** | — |
| Is $L$ inherently ambiguous? | — | — | undecidable | — |
| Is $L_1 \cap L_2$ context-free? | — | — | undecidable | — |

The pattern to carry into the exam: **for regular languages everything is decidable**; for CFLs the *one-grammar* questions (empty, finite, membership) are decidable while the *two-grammar* and "is it simpler than it looks" questions are undecidable; for CSLs only membership survives; for RE almost nothing does.

The undecidable CFL questions are proved by reduction from PCP: given a PCP instance you build two grammars whose intersection is non-empty exactly when the instance has a solution, and whose combination is ambiguous exactly when it has a solution.

## Tractable and intractable

Undecidable problems have no algorithm at all. Intractable problems have algorithms whose running time makes them useless. The complexity classes separate the two kinds of bad news.

- **P** — decidable by a deterministic TM in time $O(n^{k})$ for some fixed $k$. The working definition of "tractable".
- **NP** — decidable by a *non-deterministic* TM in polynomial time; equivalently, every yes-instance has a **certificate** of polynomial size that a deterministic verifier checks in polynomial time. NP stands for **non-deterministic polynomial**, never for "non-polynomial".
- **co-NP** — the complements of NP languages; a *no*-instance has a short checkable certificate.
- **NP-hard** — every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time. An NP-hard problem need not be in NP and need not even be decidable: the halting problem is NP-hard.
- **NP-complete** — in NP **and** NP-hard. These are the hardest problems in NP, and they stand or fall together: if any one is in P, then P $=$ NP.
- **PSPACE** — decidable in polynomial space. Savitch's theorem gives PSPACE $=$ NPSPACE.

Known containments:

$$\text{L} \subseteq \text{NL} \subseteq \text{P} \subseteq \text{NP} \subseteq \text{PSPACE} \subseteq \text{EXPTIME}$$

Every inclusion shown is believed strict but only $\text{P} \subsetneq \text{EXPTIME}$ and $\text{NL} \subsetneq \text{PSPACE}$ are proved. Whether P $=$ NP is open, as is NP $=$ co-NP. Note P $\subseteq$ NP $\cap$ co-NP, so if any NP-complete problem is in co-NP then NP $=$ co-NP.

**Cook-Levin theorem.** SAT is NP-complete — the first such proof, done directly by encoding an NP machine's computation as a Boolean formula. Every later NP-completeness proof is a polynomial reduction from an already-known NP-complete problem.

| In P | NP-complete | Open / harder |
|---|---|---|
| 2-SAT, Horn-SAT | SAT, 3-SAT, CNF-SAT | Graph isomorphism (unknown) |
| Shortest path, MST | Clique, Vertex cover, Independent set | Integer factoring (unknown) |
| Euler circuit | Hamiltonian cycle, TSP (decision) | QBF / TQBF (PSPACE-complete) |
| Bipartite matching | Subset sum, Partition, 0/1 knapsack | Halting problem (undecidable, NP-hard) |
| Primality (AKS), Linear programming | Graph 3-colouring, Set cover, Bin packing | |

Note the deliberate near-misses: 2-SAT is in P but 3-SAT is NP-complete; Euler circuit is in P but Hamiltonian cycle is NP-complete; 2-colouring (bipartiteness) is in P but 3-colouring is NP-complete; fractional knapsack is greedy and polynomial but 0/1 knapsack is NP-complete. Those four pairs supply a large share of the questions asked on this topic.

blocks.title: The four sentences students get backwards
blocks.text:
1. **NP does not mean "not polynomial".** It means non-deterministic polynomial, and $\text{P} \subseteq \text{NP}$, so every tractable problem is in NP.
2. **NP-hard does not imply NP-complete.** Completeness additionally requires membership in NP. The halting problem is NP-hard and not in NP.
3. **To prove $B$ is NP-hard, reduce a known NP-hard $A$ *to* $B$**, i.e. $A \le_p B$. Reducing $B$ to SAT proves $B$ is *in* NP, which is the opposite claim.
4. **Undecidable and intractable are different.** An intractable problem has an algorithm that is too slow; an undecidable one has no algorithm. Presburger arithmetic is decidable and doubly-exponentially intractable; the halting problem is neither.

blocks.q: Which of these problems about a Turing machine $M$ is **decidable**?
opts: Does $M$ halt on the empty input within 50 steps?
Does $M$ accept at least one string of length 3?
blocks.exp: Options 1, 2 and 4 are non-trivial properties of the *language* $L(M)$, so Rice's theorem makes them undecidable. Option 3 is a property of the machine's behaviour over a bounded horizon: simulate 50 steps and report — the simulation always terminates, so it is decidable. The bound is what saves it; 'does $M$ halt on the empty input' with no bound is undecidable.

blocks.q: $L_1$ and $L_2$ are context-free grammars' languages. Which question is decidable?
blocks.exp: Finiteness is decidable: put the grammar in CNF, remove useless symbols, and check the variable dependency graph for a cycle — a cycle means infinitely many strings. Equivalence, disjointness of intersection and universality are all undecidable for CFLs, each by reduction from PCP. The rule of thumb is that single-grammar structural questions (empty, finite, membership) are decidable and comparisons between two grammars are not.

blocks.q: A problem $X$ is NP-complete. Which statement follows?
opts: $X$ cannot be solved by any algorithm
$X \in$ NP and every problem in NP reduces to $X$ in polynomial time
$X$ is NP-hard but not necessarily in NP
blocks.exp: NP-complete means exactly two things at once: membership in NP, and NP-hardness (every NP problem polynomial-time reduces to it). NP-complete problems are all decidable, by definition of NP. Whether they are in P is the open P vs NP question, and option 4 describes NP-hardness alone.

blocks.q: To prove that a new problem $B$ is undecidable, the correct reduction is:
blocks.exp: A reduction $A \le_m B$ says 'a decider for $B$ would give a decider for $A$'. Taking $A$ = halting problem, a decider for $B$ would decide halting, which is impossible — hence no decider for $B$. Reducing $B$ to halting only shows $B$ is no harder than halting, which every RE problem already satisfies and which proves nothing.

tricks.title: Rice's theorem test: 'is it a property of the set of accepted strings?'
tricks.body: Ask whether two machines with the *same* language must get the same answer. If yes and the property is non-trivial, it is undecidable by Rice, no proof needed. If the answer can depend on the machine's code, states or step count, Rice does not apply and the problem is usually decidable.

tricks.title: Reduction direction: the KNOWN problem goes on the LEFT
tricks.body: $\text{known undecidable} \le_m \text{new problem}$ and $\text{known NP-hard} \le_p \text{new problem}$. Say it as 'I could solve the hard old problem if I could solve the new one', and the direction never comes out wrong.

tricks.title: For CFL decidability, count the grammars in the question
tricks.body: One grammar and a structural question (empty, finite, infinite, membership): decidable. Two grammars (equality, containment, disjoint intersection) or a claim about simpler classes (is it regular, is it ambiguous, is it a DCFL): undecidable. That single heuristic answers almost every question in the table.

tricks.title: Solve PCP instances by tracking the overhang
tricks.body: After each tile, record which side leads and by what string. The instance is solvable iff you can reach overhang $\varepsilon$. If the reachable overhangs form a cycle that never includes $\varepsilon$, you have a proof of unsolvability, not just a failed search.

tricks.title: Memorise the near-miss pairs for P vs NP-complete
tricks.body: 2-SAT (P) / 3-SAT (NPC); Euler circuit (P) / Hamiltonian cycle (NPC); 2-colouring (P) / 3-colouring (NPC); fractional knapsack (P) / 0-1 knapsack (NPC); shortest path (P) / longest simple path (NPC). Questions are built from exactly these boundaries.

traps.title: RE-ness of a problem and of its complement are different questions
traps.body: HALT and $A_{TM}$ are RE but not recursive, so their complements are not RE. $E_{TM} = \{\langle M\rangle : L(M)=\varnothing\}$ is the other way round: it is *not* RE, while its complement is. Questions asking 'which of the following is not recursively enumerable' depend entirely on getting this orientation right.

traps.title: Rice's theorem does not apply to properties of the machine
traps.body: '$M$ has 17 states', '$M$ writes a blank at some point in the first 10 steps', '$M$'s transition table is symmetric' are all decidable. Applying Rice to them is the standard wrong answer. Rice is only about $L(M)$.

traps.title: NP-hard does not mean 'in NP and hard'
traps.body: It means at least as hard as everything in NP, with no upper bound implied. Undecidable problems can be NP-hard. Only NP-complete problems are guaranteed to be both in NP and maximally hard within it.

traps.title: Decidable can still be hopeless
traps.body: Context-sensitive membership is decidable and PSPACE-complete; the decision procedure for Presburger arithmetic is doubly exponential. 'Decidable' is a statement about existence of an algorithm, never about its cost, and a question contrasting decidability with tractability is testing precisely that.

topics.title: Lexical and Syntax Analysis: LL, LR and LALR Parsing
topics.summary: Tokens and lexical analysis; precedence and associativity in grammars; left-recursion removal and left factoring; FIRST, FOLLOW and LL(1) tables; LR(0) items and the canonical collection; and the precise differences between SLR(1), CLR(1) and LALR(1).

blocks.text:
## Where the front end sits

A compiler's front end turns characters into a checked syntax tree in three passes. **Lexical analysis** groups characters into tokens; **syntax analysis** (parsing) groups tokens into a tree according to a grammar; **semantic analysis** (topic 8.7) decorates the tree with types and other attributes. Errors are caught in increasing order of subtlety: `12abc` is a lexical error, `a = = b` is a syntax error, `a = b + "x"` is a semantic error.

**Lexical analysis** deals with three separate ideas that questions deliberately blur:

- a **token** is a category, e.g. `id`, `num`, `relop`, `if`;
- a **pattern** is the rule describing the category, normally a regular expression such as `letter (letter | digit)*`;
- a **lexeme** is the actual character sequence matched, e.g. `count`, `3.14`.

The lexical analyser is a DFA built from the union of all token patterns (a regular expression is converted to an NFA by Thompson's construction, then determinised and minimised). Two tie-breaking rules resolve the ambiguity that results from unioning patterns:

1. **Longest match** — prefer the longest lexeme. This is why `<=` is one token, not `<` followed by `=`, and why `intx` is one identifier, not the keyword `int` followed by `x`.
2. **Rule priority** — among matches of equal length, the pattern listed first wins. This is how keywords are separated from identifiers, since `if` matches both patterns with the same length.

Because token patterns are regular, the lexer needs no stack; the parser needs one, which is exactly the regular-versus-context-free boundary of topic 8.3. Practical lexers use a two-buffer scheme with sentinels so that a single test detects both "buffer exhausted" and "end of input", and they hand the parser a stream of `(token, attribute)` pairs while entering identifiers into the symbol table.

## Precedence and associativity in the grammar

The grammar itself encodes how expressions group. The mechanism is entirely structural:

- **One non-terminal per precedence level**, with the tightest-binding operator at the deepest level. Deeper means nearer the leaves, hence evaluated first.
- **Left recursion gives left associativity**; right recursion gives right associativity.

For $+$ and $*$ with the usual precedence, $+$ and $*$ left-associative:

$$E \to E + T \mid T, \qquad T \to T * F \mid F, \qquad F \to (E) \mid \texttt{id}$$

$*$ sits one level below $+$, so it binds tighter; both rules are left recursive, so both operators associate left and $a - b - c$ parses as $(a-b)-c$. For a right-associative operator such as exponentiation or assignment, use right recursion:

$$E \to T \uparrow E \mid T$$

which makes $a \uparrow b \uparrow c$ parse as $a \uparrow (b \uparrow c)$.

The ambiguous grammar $E \to E+E \mid E*E \mid \texttt{id}$ has neither property, which is precisely why it is ambiguous. Yacc-style tools accept it anyway and resolve the conflicts with declared `%left`, `%right` and `%nonassoc` directives — equivalent to the layered grammar, but with fewer states.

The **dangling else** is the same problem in conditional form:

$$S \to \texttt{if } E \texttt{ then } S \mid \texttt{if } E \texttt{ then } S \texttt{ else } S \mid \texttt{other}$$

is ambiguous for `if E1 then if E2 then S1 else S2`. The universal convention — "match the `else` with the nearest unmatched `then`" — corresponds to **preferring shift over reduce** in an LR parser, and to rewriting the grammar with matched/unmatched statement non-terminals if you want it unambiguous outright.

## Left recursion removal and left factoring

Top-down parsers cannot handle left recursion at all: $A \to A\alpha$ makes a predictive parser expand $A$ into $A$ forever. Two mechanical transformations fix the two most common obstacles.

**Immediate left recursion.** Replace

$$A \to A\alpha_1 \mid \cdots \mid A\alpha_m \mid \beta_1 \mid \cdots \mid \beta_n$$

by

$$A \to \beta_1 A' \mid \cdots \mid \beta_n A', \qquad A' \to \alpha_1 A' \mid \cdots \mid \alpha_m A' \mid \varepsilon.$$

**Indirect left recursion.** Order the non-terminals $A_1, \ldots, A_n$. For $i = 1$ to $n$: for $j = 1$ to $i-1$, replace every production $A_i \to A_j\gamma$ by $A_i \to \delta\gamma$ for each $A_j \to \delta$; then eliminate the immediate left recursion in $A_i$. The algorithm requires the grammar to have no $\varepsilon$-productions and no cycles $A \Rightarrow^{+} A$.

**Left factoring.** When two alternatives share a prefix, a predictive parser cannot choose between them. Replace

$$A \to \alpha\beta_1 \mid \alpha\beta_2 \mid \gamma \qquad\text{by}\qquad A \to \alpha A' \mid \gamma, \quad A' \to \beta_1 \mid \beta_2.$$

Both transformations preserve the language exactly, but left-recursion removal **changes the parse tree shape**: the new grammar is right recursive, so the natural tree is right leaning even though the operator is left associative. Getting left associativity back requires the semantic actions of topic 8.7 to thread a value through the $A'$ chain as an *inherited* attribute — the main reason L-attributed definitions exist.

Neither transformation is a cure-all. Removing left recursion and left factoring does **not** guarantee an LL(1) grammar, and some languages have no LL(1) grammar at all.

blocks.title: Worked example — removing left recursion and left factoring
blocks.text:
**(a) Immediate.** $E \to E + T \mid T$, $T \to T * F \mid F$, $F \to (E) \mid \texttt{id}$.

For $E$: $\alpha_1 = {+}T$, $\beta_1 = T$. So

$$E \to T E', \qquad E' \to +TE' \mid \varepsilon.$$

For $T$: $\alpha_1 = {*}F$, $\beta_1 = F$. So

$$T \to F T', \qquad T' \to *FT' \mid \varepsilon.$$

$F$ has no left recursion. The result is the standard LL(1) expression grammar used below.

**(b) Indirect.** $S \to Aa \mid b$, $A \to Ac \mid Sd \mid \varepsilon$.

Order $A_1 = S$, $A_2 = A$. $S$ has no immediate left recursion, so nothing happens at $i=1$. At $i=2$, $j=1$: replace $A \to Sd$ using $S \to Aa \mid b$:

$$A \to Ac \mid Aad \mid bd \mid \varepsilon.$$

Now eliminate the immediate left recursion, with $\alpha_1 = c$, $\alpha_2 = ad$ and $\beta_1 = bd$, $\beta_2 = \varepsilon$:

$$A \to bdA' \mid A', \qquad A' \to cA' \mid adA' \mid \varepsilon.$$

Final grammar: $S \to Aa \mid b$; $A \to bdA' \mid A'$; $A' \to cA' \mid adA' \mid \varepsilon$. (Note the $\varepsilon$ alternative of the original $A$ becomes the bare $A'$ alternative, since $\beta_2 = \varepsilon$ contributes $\varepsilon A' = A'$.)

**(c) Left factoring.** $S \to \texttt{if } E \texttt{ then } S \texttt{ else } S \mid \texttt{if } E \texttt{ then } S \mid a$.

The common prefix is $\texttt{if } E \texttt{ then } S$:

$$S \to \texttt{if } E \texttt{ then } S\,S' \mid a, \qquad S' \to \texttt{else } S \mid \varepsilon.$$

The grammar is now left factored but **still ambiguous** in effect — the LL(1) table will have two entries for $S'$ on `else`, which is the dangling-else conflict resurfacing. Left factoring removes the prefix problem, not the ambiguity.

## FIRST and FOLLOW

These two sets drive every predictive parse table, and they are computed by different rules for different reasons, which is why they are so easy to confuse.

**$\text{FIRST}(\alpha)$** is the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from $\alpha$, plus $\varepsilon$ if $\alpha \Rightarrow^{*} \varepsilon$.

1. $\text{FIRST}(a) = \{a\}$ for a terminal $a$; $\text{FIRST}(\varepsilon) = \{\varepsilon\}$.
2. For $A \to Y_1 Y_2 \cdots Y_k$: add $\text{FIRST}(Y_1) - \{\varepsilon\}$ to $\text{FIRST}(A)$; if $\varepsilon \in \text{FIRST}(Y_1)$, also add $\text{FIRST}(Y_2) - \{\varepsilon\}$, and so on; if every $Y_i$ is nullable, add $\varepsilon$.

**$\text{FOLLOW}(A)$** is the set of terminals that can appear immediately to the right of $A$ in some sentential form. It is defined for **non-terminals only**, and **$\varepsilon$ is never in a FOLLOW set**.

1. Put $\$$ (end marker) in $\text{FOLLOW}(S)$ for the start symbol $S$.
2. For $A \to \alpha B \beta$: add $\text{FIRST}(\beta) - \{\varepsilon\}$ to $\text{FOLLOW}(B)$.
3. For $A \to \alpha B$, or $A \to \alpha B \beta$ with $\varepsilon \in \text{FIRST}(\beta)$: add $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$ to $\text{FOLLOW}(B)$.

Iterate rules until nothing changes. Compute **all** FIRST sets before starting FOLLOW, and compute FOLLOW sets in an order that respects rule 3's dependencies (or just iterate to a fixed point).

**The LL(1) table.** For each production $A \to \alpha$:

- for every terminal $a \in \text{FIRST}(\alpha)$, put $A \to \alpha$ in $M[A, a]$;
- if $\varepsilon \in \text{FIRST}(\alpha)$, then for every $b \in \text{FOLLOW}(A)$ put $A \to \alpha$ in $M[A, b]$.

The grammar is **LL(1)** iff no cell ends up with two entries. Equivalently, for every pair of alternatives $A \to \alpha \mid \beta$: $\text{FIRST}(\alpha) \cap \text{FIRST}(\beta) = \varnothing$, and if $\beta \Rightarrow^{*} \varepsilon$ then $\text{FIRST}(\alpha) \cap \text{FOLLOW}(A) = \varnothing$.

blocks.title: Worked example — FIRST, FOLLOW and the LL(1) table
blocks.text:
$$E \to TE', \quad E' \to +TE' \mid \varepsilon, \quad T \to FT', \quad T' \to *FT' \mid \varepsilon, \quad F \to (E) \mid \texttt{id}$$

**FIRST sets.**

- $\text{FIRST}(F) = \{(, \texttt{id}\}$ directly from its two bodies.
- $T \to FT'$, and $F$ is not nullable, so $\text{FIRST}(T) = \text{FIRST}(F) = \{(, \texttt{id}\}$.
- $E \to TE'$, likewise $\text{FIRST}(E) = \{(, \texttt{id}\}$.
- $\text{FIRST}(T') = \{*, \varepsilon\}$; $\text{FIRST}(E') = \{+, \varepsilon\}$.

**FOLLOW sets.**

- $\text{FOLLOW}(E) = \{\$\}$ initially. From $F \to (E)$, the symbol after $E$ is the terminal $)$, so rule 2 adds it. So $\text{FOLLOW}(E) = \{), \$\}$.
- From $E \to TE'$, $E'$ is last, so rule 3 gives $\text{FOLLOW}(E') \supseteq \text{FOLLOW}(E) = \{), \$\}$. Also $E' \to +TE'$ ends in $E'$, adding nothing new. $\text{FOLLOW}(E') = \{), \$\}$.
- From $E \to TE'$, rule 2 gives $\text{FOLLOW}(T) \supseteq \text{FIRST}(E') - \{\varepsilon\} = \{+\}$; since $\varepsilon \in \text{FIRST}(E')$, rule 3 adds $\text{FOLLOW}(E) = \{), \$\}$. From $E' \to +TE'$, the same two contributions. $\text{FOLLOW}(T) = \{+, ), \$\}$.
- From $T \to FT'$, $T'$ is last: $\text{FOLLOW}(T') \supseteq \text{FOLLOW}(T) = \{+, ), \$\}$. $\text{FOLLOW}(T') = \{+, ), \$\}$.
- From $T \to FT'$, rule 2 gives $\text{FOLLOW}(F) \supseteq \text{FIRST}(T') - \{\varepsilon\} = \{*\}$; $\varepsilon \in \text{FIRST}(T')$ so rule 3 adds $\text{FOLLOW}(T) = \{+,),\$\}$. $\text{FOLLOW}(F) = \{*, +, ), \$\}$.

Summary:

| $X$ | FIRST$(X)$ | FOLLOW$(X)$ |
|---|---|---|
| $E$ | $\{(, \texttt{id}\}$ | $\{), \$\}$ |
| $E'$ | $\{+, \varepsilon\}$ | $\{), \$\}$ |
| $T$ | $\{(, \texttt{id}\}$ | $\{+, ), \$\}$ |
| $T'$ | $\{*, \varepsilon\}$ | $\{+, ), \$\}$ |
| $F$ | $\{(, \texttt{id}\}$ | $\{*, +, ), \$\}$ |

**Parse table.** Blank cells are errors.

| | $\texttt{id}$ | $+$ | $*$ | $($ | $)$ | $\$$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $E$ | $E \to TE'$ | | | $E \to TE'$ | | |
| $E'$ | | $E' \to +TE'$ | | | $E' \to \varepsilon$ | $E' \to \varepsilon$ |
| $T$ | $T \to FT'$ | | | $T \to FT'$ | | |
| $T'$ | | $T' \to \varepsilon$ | $T' \to *FT'$ | | $T' \to \varepsilon$ | $T' \to \varepsilon$ |
| $F$ | $F \to \texttt{id}$ | | | $F \to (E)$ | | |

No cell has two entries, so the grammar is **LL(1)**. Notice where the $\varepsilon$-productions landed: $E' \to \varepsilon$ went into the columns of $\text{FOLLOW}(E') = \{),\$\}$, not into any FIRST column — that is rule 2 of the table construction, and putting it in the wrong columns is the commonest way to lose the question.

**A parse of $\texttt{id} + \texttt{id} * \texttt{id}$.** Stack (top left) against remaining input:

| Stack | Input | Action |
|---|---|---|
| $E\$$ | $\texttt{id}+\texttt{id}*\texttt{id}\$$ | $E \to TE'$ |
| $TE'\$$ | $\texttt{id}+\ldots$ | $T \to FT'$ |
| $FT'E'\$$ | $\texttt{id}+\ldots$ | $F \to \texttt{id}$ |
| $\texttt{id}T'E'\$$ | $\texttt{id}+\ldots$ | match |
| $T'E'\$$ | $+\texttt{id}*\texttt{id}\$$ | $T' \to \varepsilon$ (since $+ \in \text{FOLLOW}(T')$) |
| $E'\$$ | $+\texttt{id}*\texttt{id}\$$ | $E' \to +TE'$ |
| $+TE'\$$ | $+\ldots$ | match |
| $TE'\$$ | $\texttt{id}*\texttt{id}\$$ | $T \to FT'$, $F \to \texttt{id}$, match |
| $T'E'\$$ | $*\texttt{id}\$$ | $T' \to *FT'$ |
| $*FT'E'\$$ | $*\texttt{id}\$$ | match, $F \to \texttt{id}$, match |
| $T'E'\$$ | $\$$ | $T' \to \varepsilon$, $E' \to \varepsilon$ |
| $\$$ | $\$$ | accept |

blocks.note: Type a grammar, watch the FIRST and FOLLOW sets converge rule by rule, and see which cells collide.

blocks.text:
## Recursive descent and predictive parsing

**Recursive descent** writes one function per non-terminal; the function body follows the production, calling other functions for non-terminals and matching terminals against the input. In its general form it must **backtrack** when an alternative fails, which makes it exponential in the worst case and impossible to combine with side effects such as symbol-table insertion.

**Predictive parsing** is recursive descent without backtracking: the current non-terminal and the single lookahead token uniquely determine the production, which is exactly the LL(1) condition. It can be written as recursive functions, or driven by the table above with an explicit stack — the **non-recursive predictive parser**, whose driver is:

- if the stack top is a terminal, match it against the lookahead and pop both;
- if it is a non-terminal $A$ with lookahead $a$, replace $A$ by the right side of $M[A,a]$, pushed in **reverse** so the leftmost symbol ends on top;
- a blank cell is a syntax error.

LL(1) parsers build a **leftmost** derivation, top down, and the stack always holds the unmatched part of the current sentential form. The first $L$ is "scan left to right", the second is "leftmost derivation", and the $1$ is the lookahead count.

Structural facts about LL(1) grammars, each of which is a one-line question:

- No **left-recursive** grammar is LL(1) (the FIRST sets of $A \to A\alpha$ and $A \to \beta$ overlap).
- No **ambiguous** grammar is LL(1), or LR($k$) for any $k$.
- A grammar with two alternatives sharing a prefix is not LL(1) until left factored.
- An LL(1) grammar cannot have two nullable alternatives for the same non-terminal.

## LR(0) items and the canonical collection

Bottom-up parsers build a **rightmost derivation in reverse**, shifting tokens onto a stack and reducing handles. The state machine that recognises viable prefixes is built from items.

An **LR(0) item** is a production with a dot marking how much has been seen: $A \to \alpha \cdot \beta$. The dot at the far right, $A \to \alpha\cdot$, means the whole body is on the stack and a reduction is possible.

Start by **augmenting** the grammar with $S' \to S$, so that acceptance is a single, unambiguous event.

**CLOSURE($I$)**: while some item $A \to \alpha \cdot B\beta$ is in $I$ and $B \to \gamma$ is a production, add $B \to \cdot\gamma$. (Intuition: if you are about to see a $B$, you are about to see any of its bodies from the start.)

**GOTO($I$, $X$)**: closure of $\{A \to \alpha X \cdot \beta \mid A \to \alpha \cdot X\beta \in I\}$ — advance the dot past $X$.

The **canonical LR(0) collection** starts from $I_0 = \text{CLOSURE}(\{S' \to \cdot S\})$ and closes under GOTO on every grammar symbol. Each item set becomes a parser state; GOTO on terminals fills the ACTION table's shift entries, GOTO on non-terminals fills the GOTO table.

Filling in the reductions is where the four LR variants differ, and the difference is **only the lookahead used to decide when to reduce**:

| Parser | Reduce $A \to \alpha$ in a state containing $A \to \alpha\cdot$ on which lookaheads? |
|---|---|
| **LR(0)** | all terminals — so any state with both a complete and an incomplete item conflicts |
| **SLR(1)** | on $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$ — a global approximation |
| **CLR(1) = LR(1)** | on the lookahead carried inside the LR(1) item, computed per state — exact |
| **LALR(1)** | on the union of lookaheads of the LR(1) states that share the same core |

blocks.title: Worked example — canonical collection, SLR(1) table, and the LALR merge
blocks.text:
Grammar, augmented: $(0)\ S' \to S$; $(1)\ S \to CC$; $(2)\ C \to cC$; $(3)\ C \to d$.

**LR(0) canonical collection.**

- $I_0 = \{S' \to \cdot S,\ S \to \cdot CC,\ C \to \cdot cC,\ C \to \cdot d\}$
- $I_1 = \text{GOTO}(I_0,S) = \{S' \to S\cdot\}$
- $I_2 = \text{GOTO}(I_0,C) = \{S \to C\cdot C,\ C \to \cdot cC,\ C \to \cdot d\}$
- $I_3 = \text{GOTO}(I_0,c) = \{C \to c\cdot C,\ C \to \cdot cC,\ C \to \cdot d\}$
- $I_4 = \text{GOTO}(I_0,d) = \{C \to d\cdot\}$
- $I_5 = \text{GOTO}(I_2,C) = \{S \to CC\cdot\}$
- $I_6 = \text{GOTO}(I_3,C) = \{C \to cC\cdot\}$

with $\text{GOTO}(I_2,c) = I_3$, $\text{GOTO}(I_2,d) = I_4$, $\text{GOTO}(I_3,c) = I_3$, $\text{GOTO}(I_3,d) = I_4$. **Seven states.**

**SLR(1) table.** $\text{FOLLOW}(S') = \text{FOLLOW}(S) = \{\$\}$ and $\text{FOLLOW}(C) = \{c, d, \$\}$.

| state | $c$ | $d$ | $\$$ | $S$ | $C$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | s3 | s4 | | 1 | 2 |
| 1 | | | acc | | |
| 2 | s3 | s4 | | | 5 |
| 3 | s3 | s4 | | | 6 |
| 4 | r3 | r3 | r3 | | |
| 5 | | | r1 | | |
| 6 | r2 | r2 | r2 | | |

No cell holds two actions, so the grammar is **SLR(1)**.

**Canonical LR(1).** Items now carry a lookahead, written $[A \to \alpha\cdot\beta,\ a]$. Closure of $[A \to \alpha\cdot B\beta, a]$ adds $[B \to \cdot\gamma, b]$ for every $b \in \text{FIRST}(\beta a)$.

- $I_0 = \{[S'\to\cdot S,\$],\ [S\to\cdot CC,\$],\ [C\to\cdot cC, c/d],\ [C\to\cdot d, c/d]\}$ — the lookaheads $c,d$ come from $\text{FIRST}(C\$) = \{c,d\}$.
- $I_2 = \text{GOTO}(I_0,C) = \{[S\to C\cdot C,\$],\ [C\to\cdot cC,\$],\ [C\to\cdot d,\$]\}$ — here the lookahead is $\$$, because the second $C$ is followed by end of input.
- $I_3 = \text{GOTO}(I_0,c) = \{[C\to c\cdot C, c/d],\ [C\to\cdot cC, c/d],\ [C\to\cdot d, c/d]\}$
- $I_4 = \text{GOTO}(I_0,d) = \{[C\to d\cdot, c/d]\}$
- $I_6 = \text{GOTO}(I_2,c) = \{[C\to c\cdot C,\$],\ [C\to\cdot cC,\$],\ [C\to\cdot d,\$]\}$
- $I_7 = \text{GOTO}(I_2,d) = \{[C\to d\cdot, \$]\}$
- $I_8 = \text{GOTO}(I_3,C) = \{[C\to cC\cdot, c/d]\}$, $I_9 = \text{GOTO}(I_6,C) = \{[C\to cC\cdot, \$]\}$
- plus $I_1 = \{[S'\to S\cdot,\$]\}$ and $I_5 = \{[S\to CC\cdot,\$]\}$

**Ten states.** The CLR parser reduces $C \to d$ on $\{c,d\}$ in state 4 but only on $\$$ in state 7 — strictly more precise than SLR, which reduces on all of $\text{FOLLOW}(C) = \{c,d,\$\}$ in both.

**LALR(1).** Merge states with the same **core** (the items ignoring lookaheads): $I_3$ with $I_6$, $I_4$ with $I_7$, $I_8$ with $I_9$. Each merged state takes the union of the lookaheads, giving $\{C \to d\cdot,\ c/d/\$\}$ and so on. The result is **seven states again** — the same count as LR(0)/SLR — with no new conflicts. This grammar is therefore LR(0)-parsable in structure, SLR(1), LALR(1) and CLR(1).

## SLR, CLR and LALR: the exact differences

All three share the same **shift** behaviour and the same viable-prefix automaton shape. They differ only in the reduce entries.

**SLR(1)** is the weakest because $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$ is computed once for the whole grammar and ignores the context in which the state was reached. The standard failure:

$$S' \to S, \quad S \to L = R \mid R, \quad L \to *R \mid \texttt{id}, \quad R \to L$$

The state containing $\{S \to L\cdot = R,\ R \to L\cdot\}$ can shift on $=$ (from the first item) and, since $= \in \text{FOLLOW}(R)$, can also reduce $R \to L$ — a **shift-reduce conflict**. The grammar is nevertheless unambiguous and is LALR(1) and CLR(1), because the exact lookahead for $R \to L$ in that state is $\$$, not $=$. This example is the standard proof that SLR(1) $\subsetneq$ LALR(1).

**CLR(1)** is exact but expensive: for a real language grammar it can have several thousand states.

**LALR(1)** merges CLR states with identical cores. The consequences are precise and heavily examined:

- LALR(1) always has **exactly as many states as LR(0) and SLR(1)** — merging restores the LR(0) core count.
- Merging can create a **reduce-reduce conflict**, because two reductions whose lookaheads were disjoint in separate states may overlap once unioned.
- Merging can **never** create a shift-reduce conflict. A shift entry depends only on the core, which is unchanged by merging; if a merged state had a shift-reduce conflict, one of the original states already had it.
- On an erroneous input, LALR may perform **extra reductions** before announcing the error, but it never shifts a wrong symbol, so it reports the error at the same input position as CLR.

The classic grammar that is LR(1) but not LALR(1):

$$S \to aAd \mid bBd \mid aBe \mid bAe, \qquad A \to c, \qquad B \to c$$

After $a\,c$ the exact lookaheads are $\{d\}$ for $A \to c$ and $\{e\}$ for $B \to c$; after $b\,c$ they are $\{e\}$ and $\{d\}$. Both states have the core $\{A \to c\cdot,\ B \to c\cdot\}$, so LALR merges them, and each reduction now has lookaheads $\{d,e\}$ — a **reduce-reduce conflict** on both $d$ and $e$.

**The hierarchy of grammar classes** (strict at every step):

$$\text{LL(0)} \subsetneq \text{LL(1)} \subsetneq \text{LR(1)}, \qquad \text{LR(0)} \subsetneq \text{SLR(1)} \subsetneq \text{LALR(1)} \subsetneq \text{CLR(1)} = \text{LR(1)}$$

and every LL(1) grammar is LR(1), but not every LL(1) grammar is SLR(1) and not every SLR(1) grammar is LL(1) — the two families are incomparable at the same level. For *languages* rather than grammars, LR(1) languages are exactly the DCFLs, and LALR(1) and CLR(1) describe the same class of languages even though they differ on grammars.

blocks.title: Counting states without building the table
blocks.text:
Common numerical questions and their shortcuts:

- **Number of LR(0) items** for a production with body of length $k$: $k+1$ (dot in $k+1$ positions), except $A \to \varepsilon$, which yields exactly one item $A \to \cdot$. Total items $= \sum (|\text{body}| + 1)$ over all productions of the augmented grammar.
- **Number of states**: LR(0) $=$ SLR(1) $=$ LALR(1), always. CLR(1) $\ge$ that, usually strictly more.
- **Table sizes**: ACTION has (states $\times$ terminals including $\$$) cells; GOTO has (states $\times$ non-terminals) cells.

blocks.q: For the grammar $S \to aSb \mid \varepsilon$, what is $\text{FOLLOW}(S)$?
blocks.exp: Rule 1 puts $\$$ in $\text{FOLLOW}(S)$ because $S$ is the start symbol. In the body $aSb$, the symbol after $S$ is the terminal $b$, so rule 2 adds $b$. Nothing else contributes, giving $\{b,\$\}$. Note $\varepsilon$ is never a member of a FOLLOW set even though $S$ is nullable — that is a FIRST-set phenomenon only.

blocks.q: Which conflict can LALR(1) table construction introduce that is not present in the corresponding CLR(1) table?
blocks.exp: LALR merges CLR states with identical cores and unions their lookahead sets. Shift entries come from the core, which merging leaves unchanged, so a shift-reduce conflict in a merged state must already have existed in one of the originals. But two complete items whose lookaheads were disjoint across the two states may overlap after the union, creating a new reduce-reduce conflict — as in $S \to aAd \mid bBd \mid aBe \mid bAe$, $A \to c$, $B \to c$.

blocks.q: A grammar contains the productions $A \to A\alpha \mid \beta$. Which statement is correct?
opts: It is not LL(1), but it may be SLR(1)
It is not LR(1) either, because left recursion breaks bottom-up parsing too
It is LL(1) after left factoring
blocks.exp: Left recursion makes a predictive parser expand $A$ forever, and formally $\text{FIRST}(A\alpha) \supseteq \text{FIRST}(\beta)$, so the two alternatives collide in the LL(1) table. Bottom-up parsers have no such problem — they consume $\beta$ and then reduce repeatedly — so left-recursive grammars are routinely SLR(1) or LALR(1). Left factoring addresses shared prefixes, not left recursion, and left recursion by itself does not imply ambiguity.

blocks.q: A grammar has productions $S \to AB$, $A \to a$, $B \to b$ and is augmented with $S' \to S$. How many LR(0) items does it have in total?
blocks.exp: A production with a body of length $k$ contributes $k+1$ items. $S' \to S$ gives 2, $S \to AB$ gives 3, $A \to a$ gives 2, $B \to b$ gives 2, so $2+3+2+2 = 9$. (Items are not states; the canonical collection groups them into far fewer sets.)

blocks.q: In a non-recursive predictive parser, when the top of stack is non-terminal $A$, the lookahead is $a$, and $M[A,a] = A \to XYZ$, the parser
opts: pushes $X$, $Y$, $Z$ in that order after popping $A$
pops $A$ and pushes $Z$, $Y$, $X$ so that $X$ is on top
blocks.exp: The stack holds the unexpanded part of the sentential form with its leftmost symbol on top, so the body must be pushed in reverse order. The input is not consumed by an expansion — only a terminal match consumes input. FOLLOW matters only when the chosen production is the $\varepsilon$-production.

tricks.title: FOLLOW never contains $\varepsilon$; FIRST may
tricks.body: FIRST answers 'what can start this string', and the string may be empty. FOLLOW answers 'what real terminal can come next', and 'nothing' is represented by $\$$, not by $\varepsilon$. Any answer option putting $\varepsilon$ in a FOLLOW set is wrong by definition.

tricks.title: Compute FOLLOW in reverse dependency order
tricks.body: FOLLOW of a non-terminal that appears at the end of a body depends on FOLLOW of the left side. Do the start symbol first, then non-terminals that appear only inside bodies you have already finished, and you will reach the fixed point in one pass instead of iterating.

tricks.title: $\varepsilon$-productions go into FOLLOW columns of the table
tricks.body: For $A \to \alpha$ with $\varepsilon \in \text{FIRST}(\alpha)$, the entry goes in $M[A,b]$ for every $b \in \text{FOLLOW}(A)$ — never in a FIRST column. Half of all wrong LL(1) tables come from this one rule.

tricks.title: State counts: LR(0) = SLR(1) = LALR(1) < CLR(1)
tricks.body: If a question gives you the LR(0) state count and asks for LALR, the answer is the same number with no work. Only CLR(1) can be larger, because it splits states that differ in lookahead.

tricks.title: Test LL(1) pairwise, not by building the whole table
tricks.body: For each non-terminal with alternatives $\alpha$ and $\beta$, check $\text{FIRST}(\alpha) \cap \text{FIRST}(\beta) = \varnothing$, and if one is nullable check that the other's FIRST misses $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$. One failing pair settles the question; there is no need to fill 30 cells.

tricks.title: Spot the parser class from the conflict
tricks.body: A shift-reduce conflict that disappears when you use exact lookaheads means the grammar is LALR/CLR but not SLR. A reduce-reduce conflict that appears only after merging same-core states means CLR but not LALR. An unavoidable conflict in CLR means the grammar is ambiguous or non-deterministic.

traps.title: FIRST and FOLLOW are not interchangeable
traps.body: FIRST is defined for any string of grammar symbols; FOLLOW only for non-terminals. FIRST can contain $\varepsilon$; FOLLOW can contain $\$$. They are used at different points of the table construction and swapping them silently produces a table that looks plausible and is wrong.

traps.title: Left factoring does not remove left recursion, and vice versa
traps.body: They fix different obstacles: a shared prefix among alternatives versus $A \Rightarrow^{+} A\alpha$. Applying one where the other is needed leaves the grammar just as un-LL(1) as before, and neither transformation guarantees LL(1) afterwards.

traps.title: Removing left recursion changes associativity in the tree
traps.body: The language is preserved, but the natural parse tree becomes right leaning. If semantic actions compute a value as they go, they must pass a partial result down through the new $A'$ non-terminal as an inherited attribute to keep left associativity — the reason L-attributed definitions matter in topic 8.7.

traps.title: LALR is not 'CLR with fewer states and no cost'
traps.body: The saving is real, but merging can introduce reduce-reduce conflicts, so some LR(1) grammars are not LALR(1). What LALR never loses is error *position*: it may make a few extra reductions, but it never shifts a symbol that CLR would reject.

traps.title: LL(1) and SLR(1) are incomparable families
traps.body: Every LL(1) grammar is LR(1), but there are LL(1) grammars that are not SLR(1) and SLR(1) grammars that are not LL(1) (any left-recursive one). A question claiming LL(1) $\subset$ SLR(1) is wrong; the chain that is correct runs LR(0) $\subset$ SLR(1) $\subset$ LALR(1) $\subset$ CLR(1).

topics.title: Semantic Analysis and Attribute Grammars
topics.summary: Syntax-directed definitions and translation schemes; synthesized versus inherited attributes; S-attributed and L-attributed definitions; dependency graphs and evaluation order; and type expressions, type equivalence and type checking.

blocks.text:
## What semantic analysis is for

Parsing answers "is this string in the language?". A great deal of what a programming language requires cannot be expressed by a context-free grammar at all: that a variable is declared before use, that the number of actual arguments matches the number of formals, that the two sides of an assignment have compatible types. These are **context-sensitive** conditions, and forcing them into the grammar would make it unusable. So compilers check them in a separate phase, driven by the parse tree.

The formal device is the **attribute grammar** (or **syntax-directed definition**, SDD): a context-free grammar in which every grammar symbol carries a set of **attributes**, and every production carries **semantic rules** that compute them. Attributes hold whatever the compiler needs — a type, a value, a symbol-table pointer, a piece of generated code, a width in bytes.

An SDD with the attribute values filled in on an actual parse tree is an **annotated parse tree**. The two questions that follow are (a) which attribute depends on which, and (b) in what order can they legally be evaluated — and those two questions are the whole topic.

## Synthesized and inherited attributes

Consider a node for production $A \to X_1 X_2 \cdots X_n$.

- A **synthesized** attribute of $A$ is computed from attributes of $A$'s **children** (and of $A$ itself). Information flows **up** the tree.
- An **inherited** attribute of a child $X_i$ is computed from attributes of its **parent** $A$, of its **siblings**, and of itself. Information flows **down and sideways**.

Terminals may have synthesized attributes only, supplied by the lexical analyser (`digit.lexval`, `id.lexeme`). Terminals never have inherited attributes. The start symbol has no inherited attributes, since it has no parent.

Which you need is decided by the direction the information travels in the language:

- Evaluating an expression: the value of a subexpression is built from its parts — **synthesized**.
- Distributing a declared type across a list of identifiers, as in `int a, b, c`: the type is known at the top of the list and must reach each identifier — **inherited**.
- Recovering left associativity after left-recursion removal: the partial result computed on the left must be handed to the tail non-terminal — **inherited**.

Two named classes of SDD matter because they are the ones that can be evaluated during a single parse:

**S-attributed**: every attribute is synthesized. Such a definition can be evaluated **bottom up**, in any bottom-up order of the tree — in particular during an LR parse, computing each node's attributes at the moment of reduction. This is exactly what Yacc and Bison implement with `$$`, `$1`, `$2`.

**L-attributed**: every attribute is either synthesized, or inherited by $X_i$ from the parent $A$ or from siblings $X_1, \ldots, X_{i-1}$ that lie strictly to its **left**, or from $X_i$'s own inherited attributes. The information never flows right to left among siblings. L-attributed definitions can be evaluated in a single **depth-first, left-to-right** traversal, which is the order a top-down (LL) parser naturally follows.

Every S-attributed definition is L-attributed, vacuously, since it has no inherited attributes to constrain. The converse fails.

blocks.title: Worked example — an S-attributed desk calculator
blocks.text:
$$L \to E\ \texttt{n}, \quad E \to E_1 + T \mid T, \quad T \to T_1 * F \mid F, \quad F \to (E) \mid \texttt{digit}$$

Semantic rules, all synthesized:

| Production | Rule |
|---|---|
| $L \to E\ \texttt{n}$ | $L.\text{val} = E.\text{val}$ |
| $E \to E_1 + T$ | $E.\text{val} = E_1.\text{val} + T.\text{val}$ |
| $E \to T$ | $E.\text{val} = T.\text{val}$ |
| $T \to T_1 * F$ | $T.\text{val} = T_1.\text{val} \times F.\text{val}$ |
| $T \to F$ | $T.\text{val} = F.\text{val}$ |
| $F \to (E)$ | $F.\text{val} = E.\text{val}$ |
| $F \to \texttt{digit}$ | $F.\text{val} = \texttt{digit}.\text{lexval}$ |

**Annotate the tree for $3 * 5 + 4\ \texttt{n}$.** Work bottom up, in the order an LR parser reduces:

1. $\texttt{digit}(3) \Rightarrow F.\text{val} = 3 \Rightarrow T.\text{val} = 3$.
2. $\texttt{digit}(5) \Rightarrow F.\text{val} = 5$.
3. $T \to T_1 * F$: $T.\text{val} = 3 \times 5 = 15$.
4. $E \to T$: $E.\text{val} = 15$.
5. $\texttt{digit}(4) \Rightarrow F.\text{val} = 4 \Rightarrow T.\text{val} = 4$.
6. $E \to E_1 + T$: $E.\text{val} = 15 + 4 = 19$.
7. $L \to E\ \texttt{n}$: $L.\text{val} = 19$.

Every rule read only its children, so the attributes could be computed exactly at reduction time, with no extra tree traversal: the definition is **S-attributed**. Note that the grammar's precedence layering is what made $3*5$ group first; the semantic rules contain no precedence logic at all.

blocks.title: Worked example — an L-attributed definition that needs inheritance
blocks.text:
Removing left recursion from $E \to E - T \mid E + T \mid T$ gives

$$E \to T E', \qquad E' \to -\,T\,E'_1 \mid +\,T\,E'_1 \mid \varepsilon, \qquad T \to \texttt{digit}$$

which is LL(1), but the tree now leans right, so a purely synthesized evaluation would compute $9-(5+2)$ instead of $(9-5)+2$. The fix is to carry the running result **down** as an inherited attribute $E'.\text{inh}$ and return the finished value **up** as $E'.\text{syn}$:

| Production | Rules |
|---|---|
| $E \to T E'$ | $E'.\text{inh} = T.\text{val}$; $E.\text{val} = E'.\text{syn}$ |
| $E' \to -\,T\,E'_1$ | $E'_1.\text{inh} = E'.\text{inh} - T.\text{val}$; $E'.\text{syn} = E'_1.\text{syn}$ |
| $E' \to +\,T\,E'_1$ | $E'_1.\text{inh} = E'.\text{inh} + T.\text{val}$; $E'.\text{syn} = E'_1.\text{syn}$ |
| $E' \to \varepsilon$ | $E'.\text{syn} = E'.\text{inh}$ |
| $T \to \texttt{digit}$ | $T.\text{val} = \texttt{digit}.\text{lexval}$ |

**Evaluate $9 - 5 + 2$.**

- $T.\text{val} = 9$, so $E'.\text{inh} = 9$ (downward).
- At $E' \to -\,T\,E'_1$ with $T.\text{val} = 5$: $E'_1.\text{inh} = 9 - 5 = 4$ (downward).
- At $E'_1 \to +\,T\,E'_2$ with $T.\text{val} = 2$: $E'_2.\text{inh} = 4 + 2 = 6$ (downward).
- At $E'_2 \to \varepsilon$: $E'_2.\text{syn} = 6$ (turn around, upward).
- $E'_1.\text{syn} = 6$, $E'.\text{syn} = 6$, $E.\text{val} = 6$.

The answer $6$ is the left-associative one, as required. Check that this is **L-attributed**: $E'_1.\text{inh}$ depends on $E'.\text{inh}$ (the parent) and on $T.\text{val}$ ($T$ is the sibling immediately to the **left** of $E'_1$). Nothing depends on a sibling to the right, so a single depth-first left-to-right pass suffices — precisely what a recursive-descent parser does if $\text{inh}$ is a parameter and $\text{syn}$ a return value.

**A second inherited-attribute classic — distributing a declared type.**

$$D \to T\,L, \quad T \to \texttt{int} \mid \texttt{real}, \quad L \to L_1,\texttt{id} \mid \texttt{id}$$

| Production | Rules |
|---|---|
| $D \to T\,L$ | $L.\text{inh} = T.\text{type}$ |
| $T \to \texttt{int}$ | $T.\text{type} = \textit{integer}$ |
| $T \to \texttt{real}$ | $T.\text{type} = \textit{real}$ |
| $L \to L_1,\texttt{id}$ | $L_1.\text{inh} = L.\text{inh}$; $\textit{addtype}(\texttt{id}.\text{entry},\ L.\text{inh})$ |
| $L \to \texttt{id}$ | $\textit{addtype}(\texttt{id}.\text{entry},\ L.\text{inh})$ |

For `real a, b, c` the type *real* is synthesized up from $T$, handed to $L$ as an inherited attribute, and passed down the chain of $L_1$ nodes so that each of `a`, `b`, `c` is entered in the symbol table with type *real*. There is no way to do this with synthesized attributes alone, because the type appears to the **left** of the identifiers that need it.

## Dependency graphs and evaluation order

To decide whether an SDD can be evaluated at all, and in what order, build the **dependency graph** of a particular annotated parse tree:

- one node per attribute instance at each parse-tree node;
- one directed edge $b \to c$ whenever a semantic rule computes $c$ using $b$.

An evaluation order is then any **topological sort** of this graph. If the graph is acyclic, a topological order exists and the attributes can be evaluated; if it contains a cycle, the SDD is **circular** on that tree and no evaluation order exists.

Testing whether an arbitrary SDD is circular (i.e. circular on *some* tree) is decidable but intrinsically exponential, which is why compilers restrict themselves to the two safe classes:

- **S-attributed** definitions are never circular; any bottom-up order works.
- **L-attributed** definitions are never circular; the depth-first left-to-right order always works.

**A small dependency graph.** For $D \to T\,L$ with $L \to \texttt{id}$ and input `int a`:

| node | attribute | depends on |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $T.\text{type}$ | (nothing — from the production $T \to \texttt{int}$) |
| 2 | $L.\text{inh}$ | 1 |
| 3 | $\texttt{id}.\text{entry}$ | (from the lexer) |
| 4 | the $\textit{addtype}$ action | 2, 3 |

Edges $1 \to 2$, $2 \to 4$, $3 \to 4$. A valid topological order is $1, 3, 2, 4$ or $3, 1, 2, 4$ — both evaluate $T.\text{type}$ before $L.\text{inh}$ and both before the action. Notice the graph has an edge pointing *down* the tree ($1 \to 2$ goes from a node's sibling to a child's attribute), which is exactly what an inherited attribute looks like and exactly what a bottom-up-only evaluator cannot handle.

## From definitions to translation schemes

A **syntax-directed definition** says *what* each attribute equals and leaves the order open. A **syntax-directed translation scheme (SDT)** fixes the order by writing program fragments, in braces, at specific positions inside the production bodies. The position is the commitment: an action written at position $k$ is executed after everything to its left has been processed.

Two implementation facts follow directly:

- **Postfix SDTs.** If all actions sit at the right end of their bodies, the scheme is exactly an S-attributed definition and can be executed by an LR parser at reduction time. This is the normal Yacc pattern.
- **Actions in the middle.** For a bottom-up parser, an action in the middle of a body has no reduction to attach to. The standard trick is to introduce a **marker non-terminal** $M \to \varepsilon$ carrying the action, so the parser reduces $M$ at exactly that point. This can, however, introduce parsing conflicts, which is why bottom-up tools prefer postfix schemes.

For L-attributed definitions the rule is: place each inherited-attribute computation for $X_i$ **immediately before** $X_i$ in the body, and each synthesized-attribute computation for the head at the **end** of the body. A recursive-descent parser then implements the scheme by passing inherited attributes as parameters and returning synthesized ones.

## Type expressions and type checking

The largest single job of semantic analysis is type checking. Types are represented as **type expressions**, built from basic types by **type constructors**:

- basic: `int`, `real`, `char`, `bool`, plus `void` and `type_error`;
- $\texttt{array}(n, T)$ — array of $n$ elements of type $T$;
- $\texttt{pointer}(T)$;
- $T_1 \times T_2$ — Cartesian product, used for argument lists and records;
- $T_1 \to T_2$ — function from $T_1$ to $T_2$;
- named types introduced by `typedef`/`type` declarations.

So `int f(char, char)` has type $\textit{char} \times \textit{char} \to \textit{int}$, and `int a[10][20]` has type $\texttt{array}(10, \texttt{array}(20, \textit{int}))$.

**Type equivalence** comes in two flavours, and the choice is a language-design decision that questions test directly:

- **Structural equivalence**: two type expressions are equivalent if they are the same basic type, or are built by the same constructor from equivalent types. Names are transparent — expanded away before comparison.
- **Name equivalence**: two types are equivalent only if they have the same name. A `typedef` creates a genuinely new, incompatible type.

Given `typedef int celsius; typedef int fahrenheit;`, structural equivalence makes `celsius` and `fahrenheit` interchangeable, while name equivalence keeps them distinct — which is usually what the programmer wanted. C uses structural equivalence for most constructed types but name equivalence for `struct` and `union` tags; Pascal and Ada lean towards name equivalence.

**Typical checking rules**, written as SDD fragments with a synthesized attribute $\text{type}$:

| Construct | Rule |
|---|---|
| $E \to \texttt{num}$ | $E.\text{type} = \textit{integer}$ |
| $E \to E_1 + E_2$ | if $E_1.\text{type} = E_2.\text{type} = \textit{integer}$ then $\textit{integer}$ else $\ldots$ else $\textit{type\_error}$ |
| $E \to E_1[E_2]$ | if $E_2.\text{type} = \textit{integer}$ and $E_1.\text{type} = \texttt{array}(s,t)$ then $t$ else $\textit{type\_error}$ |
| $E \to \texttt{*}E_1$ | if $E_1.\text{type} = \texttt{pointer}(t)$ then $t$ else $\textit{type\_error}$ |
| $E \to E_1(E_2)$ | if $E_1.\text{type} = s \to t$ and $E_2.\text{type} = s$ then $t$ else $\textit{type\_error}$ |
| $S \to \texttt{if } E \texttt{ then } S_1$ | if $E.\text{type} = \textit{boolean}$ then $S_1.\text{type}$ else $\textit{type\_error}$ |

Once a subexpression is $\textit{type\_error}$, propagate it silently rather than reporting again, so one mistake produces one message.

Three further notions that are routinely confused:

- **Coercion (implicit conversion)** — the compiler inserts a conversion, e.g. `int` to `real` in `2 + 3.5`. **Widening** coercions (narrower to wider) are usually automatic; **narrowing** ones usually require a cast.
- **Overloading** — one name, several types; resolution picks the one matching the argument types.
- **Polymorphism** — one body, many types. Parametric polymorphism is checked by **unification**, which solves type equations by substituting for type variables.

Finally, **static versus dynamic**: static checking happens at compile time and covers type rules, declaration-before-use, flow-of-control errors (`break` outside a loop) and uniqueness of declarations; dynamic checking happens at run time and covers array-bounds violations, null dereferences and checked downcasts. A language is **strongly typed** if all type errors are caught, whether statically or dynamically — strong typing is not the same as static typing.

blocks.q: Which statement about attribute types is correct?
opts: A terminal can have both synthesized and inherited attributes
Synthesized attributes of a node depend on attributes of its children; inherited attributes depend on parent and siblings
Inherited attributes always flow upwards in the parse tree
The start symbol must have at least one inherited attribute
blocks.exp: Synthesized means computed from below, inherited means computed from the parent or siblings. Terminals get their values from the lexical analyser, so they have synthesized attributes only, and the start symbol has no parent from which to inherit anything.

blocks.q: An SDD is L-attributed. Which evaluation strategy is guaranteed to work?
opts: Any bottom-up order of the parse tree
Two passes: all inherited attributes first, then all synthesized
No fixed strategy works; a topological sort must be computed per tree
blocks.exp: The L-attributed restriction says an inherited attribute of $X_i$ uses only the parent and siblings strictly to its left, so by the time a depth-first left-to-right walk reaches $X_i$, everything it needs is already computed. That is exactly the order a recursive-descent parser visits nodes in, which is why L-attributed definitions integrate with LL parsing. Pure bottom-up order works only for S-attributed definitions.

blocks.q: With `typedef int Metres; typedef int Seconds; Metres m; Seconds s;`, the assignment `m = s;` is accepted under
blocks.exp: Structural equivalence expands the names and compares the underlying type expressions, and both expand to `int`, so the assignment is legal. Name equivalence treats each typedef as a distinct new type, so `Metres` and `Seconds` are incompatible and the assignment is rejected — which is normally the point of introducing the names.

blocks.q: Why does the left-recursion-free grammar $E \to TE'$, $E' \to +TE'_1 \mid \varepsilon$ need an inherited attribute to evaluate $9-5+2$ correctly?
opts: Because the transformed grammar yields a right-leaning tree, so the partial result computed on the left must be passed down to the tail
Because synthesized attributes cannot handle arithmetic
Because LL parsers cannot compute synthesized attributes
blocks.exp: Left-recursion removal preserves the language but changes the tree shape from left leaning to right leaning. A purely synthesized evaluation on a right-leaning tree associates to the right, giving $9-(5+2)=2$ instead of $(9-5)+2=6$. Threading the running total downwards as $E'.\text{inh}$ and returning the final value as $E'.\text{syn}$ restores left associativity.

tricks.title: Decide synthesized vs inherited by asking where the information already is
tricks.body: If the value is assembled from the parts below, it is synthesized. If it is announced above or to the left and must reach nodes below or to the right — a declared type, a running total, a nesting level, an offset — it is inherited. The direction of the arrow in the dependency graph is the answer.

tricks.title: S-attributed means 'Yacc can do it in one reduction'
tricks.body: If every rule can be written using only `$1`, `$2`, ... on the right and `$$` on the left at a reduction, the SDD is S-attributed and needs no extra pass. Any rule that needs to know something about a node not yet reduced forces inheritance.

tricks.title: L-attributed test: scan the body left to right
tricks.body: For each rule computing an inherited attribute of $X_i$, check that every attribute it reads belongs to the parent, to $X_1 \ldots X_{i-1}$, or to $X_i$ itself. One reference to $X_{i+1}$ or further right breaks L-attributedness, and the definition then needs a separate pass.

tricks.title: Every S-attributed SDD is L-attributed
tricks.body: The containment is one way and it is strict. A question asking 'which of the following is true of the relationship' almost always has the answer 'S $\subset$ L'. Neither class can be circular, which is why real compilers use only these two.

tricks.title: Place actions by the attribute they compute
tricks.body: In a translation scheme, an inherited attribute of $X_i$ is computed in an action immediately before $X_i$; a synthesized attribute of the head is computed in an action at the very end of the body. Get the two positions right and the scheme is automatically executable by recursive descent.

traps.title: Terminals never have inherited attributes
traps.body: Their values come from the lexical analyser, so they are synthesized by definition. A question offering 'terminals can have inherited attributes' is offering a wrong option, however plausible it sounds given that a terminal has a parent.

traps.title: Circularity is a property of the dependency graph, not of the grammar
traps.body: An SDD may be non-circular on one tree and circular on another. That is why the general circularity test is exponential and why compilers prefer the syntactic restrictions (S- and L-attributed) that make circularity impossible by construction.

traps.title: Strong typing is not the same as static typing
traps.body: Static means checked at compile time; strong means all type errors are caught, possibly at run time. A dynamically typed language can be strongly typed, and a statically typed language with unchecked casts is not strongly typed. Questions that equate the two are testing precisely this distinction.

traps.title: Structural equivalence ignores names; name equivalence ignores structure
traps.body: Under structural equivalence two identical-looking records are the same type even with different names; under name equivalence two names are different types even with identical structure. Recursive types are the reason structural equivalence needs care — comparing them naively loops.

topics.title: Run Time System and Storage Organization
topics.summary: Run-time memory layout, activation records and calling sequences, static/stack/heap allocation, access links and displays, garbage collection, parameter-passing mechanisms compared on one program, and symbol table design.

blocks.text:
## The run-time memory picture

Compiled code has to manage its own memory, and the compiler decides the layout. A typical process image is divided into four regions, conventionally drawn with low addresses at the top:

| Region | Contents | Allocated when |
|---|---|---|
| **Code (text)** | machine instructions | compile time; fixed size |
| **Static / global** | globals, static locals, constants | compile time; fixed size and address |
| **Heap** | objects created by `new`/`malloc` | run time, on demand, arbitrary lifetime |
| **Stack** | activation records of active procedures | run time, on procedure entry |

Heap and stack are placed at opposite ends of the free space and grow **towards each other**, so that whichever needs more memory can use it; collision is stack overflow or heap exhaustion.

Three allocation strategies, each with a definite capability boundary:

- **Static allocation.** Every object has an address fixed at compile time. Simple and fast, but no recursion (a second activation would need a second copy of the locals) and no dynamically sized data. Old FORTRAN worked this way.
- **Stack allocation.** Storage is allocated on procedure entry and freed on exit, in last-in-first-out order. This supports recursion exactly because activations nest. It cannot support data whose lifetime outlives the procedure that created it.
- **Heap allocation.** Storage lives until it is explicitly freed or collected, in any order. Needed for objects returned from a procedure, for linked structures, and for closures. Costs allocation overhead and fragmentation.

The key question "why can't a language with only static allocation support recursion?" has this answer: recursion requires several simultaneously live copies of the same procedure's locals, and static allocation reserves exactly one.

## Activation records

Each procedure call pushes an **activation record** (stack frame). A conventional layout, from the top of the frame downwards:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Returned value** | space for the result handed back to the caller |
| **Actual parameters** | the arguments, placed by the caller |
| **Optional control link** | pointer to the **caller's** activation record — the *dynamic* link |
| **Optional access link** | pointer to the activation record of the lexically **enclosing** procedure — the *static* link, used to reach non-local data |
| **Saved machine status** | return address, saved registers, condition codes |
| **Local data** | the procedure's own variables |
| **Temporaries** | intermediate values of expression evaluation |

Two pointers navigate it: the **stack pointer** (top of stack) and the **frame pointer** or base pointer (a fixed point within the current frame, so locals are at constant offsets).

The **calling sequence** is split between the two parties, and the split is by design — put in the callee whatever is the same at every call site, so the code is written once:

- **Caller**: evaluate the actuals and place them in the frame, save its own machine status, and jump.
- **Callee (prologue)**: save the return address and the old frame pointer, set the new frame pointer, and allocate space for locals and temporaries.
- **Callee (epilogue)**: store the return value, restore the saved registers and the old frame pointer, and jump back.
- **Caller (after return)**: collect the return value and restore the stack pointer.

The **control link** chain reflects the sequence of calls actually made (who called whom), while the **access link** chain reflects the nesting of procedure declarations in the source text. In a language with no nested procedures, such as C, no access links are needed at all — non-locals are global and have static addresses.

## Scope, access links and displays

Two rules for resolving a non-local name:

- **Static (lexical) scope** — the name refers to the declaration in the innermost enclosing *block in the program text*. This is what almost every modern language uses, and it can be resolved at compile time.
- **Dynamic scope** — the name refers to the most recent still-active declaration in the *call chain*. This is resolvable only at run time, by walking control links.

The standard illustration:

```
int x = 1;
void show()  { print x; }
void test()  { int x = 2; show(); }
main()       { test(); }
```

Under static scope `show` prints **1**, because the `x` visible where `show` is *written* is the global. Under dynamic scope it prints **2**, because the most recent active binding of `x` is `test`'s local.

For a language with **nested procedures**, static scope needs a mechanism to find the right frame. Two options:

- **Access links.** Each frame points at the frame of its lexically enclosing procedure. To reach a variable declared $k$ levels out, follow $k$ access links. Cost: $O(k)$ per access, cheap to maintain.
- **Display.** Keep an array $d[1..n]$, where $d[i]$ points at the most recent activation record at nesting depth $i$. To reach a variable at depth $i$, index $d[i]$ directly — $O(1)$ per access. Cost: the display must be saved and restored around calls.

So the trade-off is stated compactly: access links make calls cheap and non-local access linear in the nesting difference; displays make non-local access constant and calls slightly more expensive.

## Parameter passing mechanisms

| Mechanism | What is passed | Effect on the actual |
|---|---|---|
| **Call by value** | a copy of the value | none; the formal is a local variable |
| **Call by reference** | the address (l-value), computed **once at call time** | every assignment to the formal writes the actual immediately |
| **Call by value-result** (copy-in copy-out) | a copy in, copied back on return | the actual changes only at return |
| **Call by name** | the unevaluated argument text, re-evaluated at **every** use | behaves like textual substitution with renaming |
